## modern-en · vives · 20:13

The unruly freedom of this member is very remarkable — so importunately ungovernable in its swelling and impatience when we have no need of it, and so unseasonably disobedient when we stand most in need of it; so imperiously contending in authority with the will, and with such haughty obstinacy refusing all our solicitation, both of hand and mind. And yet, though his rebellion is so universally complained of, and proof drawn from it to condemn him, if he had retained me to plead his cause, I should perhaps bring the rest of his fellow members under suspicion of conspiring against him out of pure envy at the importance and pleasure peculiar to his employment, and of having, by collusion, armed the whole world against him by maliciously charging him alone with their common offence. For let anyone consider whether there is any one part of our bodies that does not often refuse to perform its office at the will's command, and that does not often exercise its function in defiance of her command. Every one of them has passions of its own, that rouse and waken, stupefy and benumb them, without our consent. How often do involuntary movements of the face betray our inward thoughts, and disclose our most private secrets to bystanders. The same cause that animates this member also, without our knowledge, animates the lungs, the pulse, and the heart, the sight of a pleasing object imperceptibly spreading a flame through all our parts with a feverish motion. Is it only these veins and muscles that swell and slacken without the consent not only of the will but even of our knowledge? We do not command our hairs to stand on end, nor our skin to shiver with fear or desire; the hands often go to parts we do not direct them to; the tongue will be tied and the voice frozen when we do not know how to help it. When we have nothing to eat and would willingly suppress it, the appetite does not on that account stop stirring up the parts that are subject to it, no more, no less, than the other appetite we were speaking of; and likewise unseasonably leaves us when it thinks fit. The vessels that serve to discharge the belly have their own dilations and compressions, without and beyond our concurrence, just as do those that serve to purge the kidneys; and what St. Augustine offers, to vindicate the prerogative of the will, of having seen a man who could on command release his rear as often as he pleased, Vives, his commentator, further reinforces with another example from his own day — of a man who could break wind in tune. But these cases do not prove any more pure obedience in that part; for is anything commonly more tumultuous or indiscreet? To which let me add that I myself knew a man so rude and ungovernable that for forty years together he made his master vent with one continuous, uninterrupted outburst, and it is likely will do so till he dies of it. And I could heartily wish I only knew by reading how often a man's belly, by holding back a single puff, brings him to the very door of an exceedingly painful death; and that the emperor who gave free leave to break wind anywhere had at the same time given us the power to do it. But for our will, on whose behalf we are prosecuting, with how much greater probability may we reproach her herself with mutiny and sedition, for her irregularity and disobedience? Does she always will what we would have her will? Does she not often will what we forbid her to will, and to our manifest harm? Does she suffer herself, any more than the rest, to be governed and directed by the conclusions of our reason? To conclude, I should move, in defence of the gentleman my client, that in this matter his cause being inseparably and indistinctly joined with an accomplice, he alone is called in question, and that by arguments and accusations which cannot be charged on the other — whose business it is sometimes inopportunely to invite, but never to refuse, and to invite, moreover, in a tacit and quiet manner; and therefore the malice and injustice of his accusers are most plainly apparent. But however that may be, with my protest against the proceedings of the advocates and judges, nature will meanwhile proceed after her own way — who would have done well had she endowed this member with some particular privilege: the author of the sole immortal work of mortals; a divine work, according to Socrates; and love, the desire of immortality, and himself an immortal demon.

St Augustine’s commentator, who fortified his master’s example of the man who could command his rear with another, of a man who could break wind in tune.

## modern-en · charles-iv · 20:22

Magicians are no very good authority with me. But we have experimentally seen that women impart the marks of their fancy to the children they carry in the womb: witness the woman who was brought to bed of a Moor; and there was presented to Charles, the Emperor and King of Bohemia, a girl from near Pisa, all over rough and covered with hair, who her mother said was so conceived because of a picture of St. John the Baptist hanging within the curtains of her bed.

To whom a girl from near Pisa was presented, rough and covered with hair all over — conceived so, her mother said, because a picture of St John the Baptist hung inside her bed-curtains.

## modern-en · jacob · 20:23

It is the same with beasts: witness Jacob's sheep, and the hares and partridges that the snow turns white on the mountains. There was at my house, a little while ago, a cat seen watching a bird at the top of a tree: after they had for some time fixed their eyes on each other, the bird at last let herself fall, dead, into the cat's claws — either dazzled by the force of her own imagination, or drawn by some attractive power of the cat. Those addicted to the pleasures of the field have no doubt heard the story of the falconer who, having earnestly fixed his eyes on a kite in the air, laid a wager that he could bring her down by the sole power of his sight, and did so, as it was said — for the tales I borrow I lay upon the consciences of those from whom I have them. The reasonings are mine, and rest on the proofs of reason, not of experience; to which everyone is at liberty to add his own examples. Whoever has none, let him not refuse, given the number and variety of accidents, to believe that there are plenty of them; if I do not apply them well, let someone else do so for me. Likewise, in the subject I am treating — our manners and motions — testimonies and instances, however fabulous, serve as well as the true, provided they are possible; whether they really happened or not, at Rome or Paris, to John or Peter, they are still within the range of human capacity, which is enough for me. I see and make my advantage of it, in shadow as well as in substance; and among the various readings of history, I cull out the most rare and memorable to fit my own turn. There are authors whose sole aim and design is to give an account of things that have happened; mine, if I could reach it, would be to deliver what may happen. There is a just liberty in the schools, of supposing similitudes when they have none at hand. I do not, however, make any use of that privilege, and in this matter, by a religious scrupulousness, I surpass all historical authority. In the examples I bring in of what I have heard, read, done, or said, I have forbidden myself to dare to alter even the most trivial and indifferent circumstances; my conscience does not falsify a syllable; what my ignorance may do, I cannot say.

Whose sheep are Montaigne’s scriptural instance that a mother’s fancy marks what she carries.

## modern-en · sallust · 20:25

I am pressed to write the affairs of my own time by some who fancy I look on them with an eye less blinded by passion than another, and have a clearer insight into them because of the free access fortune has given me to the heads of various factions; but they do not consider that, to gain the glory of Sallust, I would not give myself the trouble — sworn enemy as I am to obligation, assiduity, and perseverance; that there is nothing so contrary to my style as a continued narrative, since I so often interrupt and cut myself short in my writing for want of breath; I have neither composition nor explanation worth anything, and I am ignorant, beyond a child, of the phrases and even the very words proper to express the most common things. And for that reason I have undertaken to say only what I can say, and have fitted my subject to my strength. Should I take someone for a guide, perhaps I would not be able to keep pace with him; and in the freedom of my liberty might deliver judgments which, on second thought and by reason's standard, would be illegitimate and punishable. Plutarch would say of what he has handed down to us, that it is the work of others — that his examples are entirely and everywhere exactly true; that they are useful to posterity and are presented with a lustre that will light the way to virtue, is his own work. It is not of such dangerous consequence, as in a medicinal drug, whether an old story be so or otherwise.

The Roman historian, whose glory Montaigne says he would not take the trouble to earn.

## modern-en · isocrates · 22:25

Whoever would disengage himself from this violent prejudice of custom would find several things received with absolute and undoubting opinion that have no other support than the grizzled head and wrinkled face of ancient usage. But the mask once off, and things being referred to the decision of truth and reason, he will find his judgment, as it were, altogether overturned, and yet restored to a much surer footing. For example, I shall ask him what can be more strange than to see a people obliged to obey laws they never understood; bound in all their domestic affairs — marriages, gifts, wills, sales, and purchases — to rules they cannot possibly know, being neither written nor published in their own language, and of which they are forced to purchase both the interpretation and the use? Not according to the ingenious opinion of Isocrates, who counselled his king to make the trades and dealings of his subjects free, frank, and profitable to them, and their quarrels and disputes burdensome, weighed down with heavy charges and penalties — but, by a prodigious opinion, to make sale of reason itself, and treat laws as merchandise. The Athenian rhetorician, who counselled his king to make his subjects’ trade free and their lawsuits expensive, and who says that defect is nearer allied to moderation than excess.

## modern-en · thyestes · 22:24

Once, taking it on myself to justify something in use among us, accepted with absolute authority for many leagues round about, and not content, as men commonly do, to establish it merely by force of law and example but inquiring still further into its origin, I found the foundation so weak that I, whose business it was to confirm others, was very near being dissatisfied myself. It is by this same prescription that Plato sets out to cure the unnatural and preposterous loves of his time, treating it as a sovereign remedy — namely, that public opinion condemns them; that poets and all other kinds of writers tell horrible stories about them; a recipe by virtue of which the most beautiful daughters no more allure their fathers' lust, nor brothers of the finest shape and figure their sisters' desire; the very fables of Thyestes, Oedipus, and Macareus, with the harmony of their song, infusing this wholesome opinion and belief into the tender brains of children. Chastity is, in truth, a great and shining virtue, the usefulness of which is sufficiently known; but to treat it, and set it off in its true value, according to nature, is as hard as it is easy to do so according to custom, laws, and precepts. The fundamental and universal reasons are of very obscure and difficult research, and our masters either lightly pass over them, or, not daring even to touch them, throw themselves into the liberty and protection of custom, where they puff themselves up and triumph to their heart's content. Those who refuse to be drawn off from this original source commit a still greater error, and deliver themselves to wild opinions — witness Chrysippus, who, in so many of his writings, scattered the little account he made of incestuous unions, with however near a relation.

One of the three fables — with Oedipus and Macareus — by which, Montaigne says following Plato, the poets put a wholesome horror of incest into children’s heads.

This very common consideration is what settled me in my place, and kept even my most extravagant and ungoverned youth under the rein, so as not to burden my shoulders with so great a weight as to make myself responsible for a science of that importance, and to dare in this what, in my better and more mature judgment, I would not have dared in the easiest and most indifferent things I had been instructed in, where the temerity of judging is of no consequence at all. If at times divine providence has gone beyond the rules to which it has necessarily bound and obliged us men, it is not to give us any dispensation to do the same. ## modern-en · thucydides · 22:33

Those who give the first shock to a state are almost naturally the first overwhelmed in its ruin. The fruits of public commotion are seldom enjoyed by the man who first set it going; he beats and disturbs the water for someone else's net. The unity and structure of this monarchy, of this grand edifice, having been ripped and torn in its old age by this thing called innovation, has since shown a rent and given sufficient admittance to such injuries. The royal majesty comes down with greater difficulty from the summit to the middle than it falls and tumbles headlong from the middle to the bottom. But if the inventors do the greater mischief, the imitators are more vicious — to follow examples whose horror and offence they have already felt and punished. And if there can be any honour in ill-doing, these last must yield to the others the glory of contriving and the courage of making the first attempt. All sorts of new disorders easily draw, from this primitive and ever-flowing fountain, examples and precedents to trouble and disrupt our government. We read in our very laws, made as a remedy for this first evil, the beginnings and pretexts of all sorts of wicked enterprises; and what Thucydides said of the civil wars of his time befalls us: that, in favour of public vices, they gave them new and more plausible names for their excuse, sweetening and disguising their true titles — which must be done, forsooth, to reform our conscience and belief:

The historian of the Peloponnesian war, cited for what happens to language in a civil war: the parties give the public vices new and more plausible names to excuse them. It is he who told Archidamus that when he had thrown Pericles the man always persuaded the spectators he had had no fall.

## modern-en · octavius · 22:54

since the ordinary discipline of a healthy state does not provide for these extraordinary accidents: it presupposes a body that holds itself up in its principal members and offices, and a common consent in its obedience and observance. A legitimate procedure is cold, heavy, and constrained, and not fit to make head against a headstrong and unbridled one. It is, to this day, cast in the dish of those two great men, Octavius and Cato, in the two civil wars of Sylla and Caesar, that they would rather suffer their country to undergo the last extremities than relieve their fellow-citizens at the expense of its laws, or be guilty of any innovation. For, in truth, in these last necessities, where there is no other remedy, it would perhaps be more prudent to stoop and yield a little, to receive the blow, than, by opposing without possibility of doing good, to give occasion to violence to trample all under foot; and better to make the laws do what they can, when they cannot do what they would. After this manner did the man who suspended them for twenty-four hours; and he who, for once, shifted a day in the calendar; and the other who, of the month of June, made a second of May. The Lacedaemonians themselves, so religious observers of the laws of their country, being constrained by one of their own edicts which expressly forbade them to choose the same man twice as admiral, and on the other hand, their affairs necessarily requiring that Lysander should again take that command upon him, they made one Aratus admiral — true enough, but with this addition, that Lysander went out as general of the navy. And by the same subtlety, one of their ambassadors being sent to the Athenians to obtain the revocation of some decree, and Pericles pointing out to him that it was forbidden to take down the tablet on which a law had once been engrossed, he advised him only to turn it round, that being not forbidden. And Plutarch praises Philopoemen for this — that, being born to command, he knew how to do it not only according to the laws but also to overrule the laws themselves, when public necessity so required.

Who with Cato is still reproached for having let his country go to the last extremity rather than relieve his fellow citizens at the expense of its laws.

## modern-en · jacques-amyot · 23:0

Jacques Amyot, grand almoner of France, one day told me a story that does great honour to one of our princes — and ours he was on several very good counts, though originally of foreign extraction. During our first commotions, at the siege of Rouen, this prince was warned by the queen-mother of a conspiracy against his life, with her letters naming the very man who was to carry it out: a gentleman of Anjou or Maine who normally frequented the prince's household. The prince did not breathe a syllable of this to anyone. The next day he went up to St Catherine's Mount, from which our battery was playing against the town (for the siege was still on), accompanied by the said lord almoner and another bishop. He saw the gentleman who had been pointed out to him, and sent for him at once. When the man came before him, already pale and trembling under the weight of his guilt, the prince said: "Monsieur So-and-so, you can guess what I have to say to you; your face gives it away. There's no point in disguising your scheme — I'm so well informed of your business that any attempt to conceal or deny it will only make things worse for you. You know perfectly well such-and-such details" (the most secret circumstances of the conspiracy), "so as you value your life, confess the whole truth of the plot." The poor man, seeing himself trapped and convicted (the whole business had been disclosed to the queen by one of the accomplices), didn't know what to do. He folded his hands, begged and pleaded for mercy, and threw himself at his prince's feet. The prince raised him up and went on: "Now, sir, tell me — have I ever offended you? Have I, out of private hatred or malice, wronged any kinsman or friend of yours? It's not even three weeks since I first laid eyes on you. What could possibly have driven you to attempt my death?" In a trembling voice the gentleman replied that it was no private grudge against him personally, but the general interest of his party; that certain people had urged him on, persuading him it would be a meritorious act, by any means available, to wipe out so great and so powerful an enemy of their religion. "Well," said the prince, "I'll show you how much more charitable my religion is than yours. Yours has counselled you to kill me, without hearing me speak, without my having given you any cause for offence; mine commands me to forgive you, even though by your own confession you stand convicted of a design to kill me without reason. Get out. Don't let me see you again. And if you're wise, choose more honest counsellors from now on for your schemes."

## modern-en · l-cinna · 23:1

The Emperor Augustus, while in Gaul, received reliable information of a conspiracy that L. Cinna was contriving against him. He resolved to make an example of the man, and to that end summoned his friends to meet in council the next morning. But the intervening night he spent in great inner agitation, considering that he was about to put to death a young man from an illustrious family, nephew to the great Pompey. The thought drove him into a series of passionate outbursts. "What then," he said, "am I to live in perpetual anxiety and alarm, and let my would-be assassin wander freely about? Will he go unpunished for having conspired against my life — a life I've defended through so many civil wars, so many battles by land and sea? After settling universal peace over the whole world, am I to pardon a man who's plotted not just to murder me but to slaughter me at sacrifice?" — for the plan was to kill him while he officiated. After a long silence he started up again, louder, raging at himself: "Why are you alive, if so many would benefit from your death? Will there be no end to your reprisals and cruelties? Is your life worth so much that so much harm must be done to preserve it?" His wife Livia, seeing him in this perplexity, said: "Will you take a woman's advice? Do as the physicians do — when the usual remedies fail, try the opposite. Severity has got you nowhere so far: Lepidus followed Salvidienus, Murena followed Lepidus, Caepio followed Murena, Egnatius followed Caepio. Try sweetness and clemency now. Cinna is convicted; pardon him. He'll never have the heart to harm you afterwards, and it'll add to your glory." Augustus was relieved to find an advocate of his own inclination. He thanked his wife, countermanded the summons to council, and ordered Cinna to be brought to him alone. When Cinna arrived, the room cleared and a chair set for him, Augustus said: "First, Cinna, I ask you to hear me out patiently. Don't interrupt — I'll give you time to answer afterwards. You know, Cinna, that I took you prisoner in the enemy's camp, where you were not merely an enemy by circumstance but an enemy by birth. I spared your life, restored all your goods, and finally set you up so comfortably by my generosity that the victors envied the defeated. The priestly office you petitioned me for, I granted you — after denying it to others whose fathers had always borne arms in my service. After all these favours, you've undertaken to kill me." Cinna cried out that he was very far from harbouring any such wicked thought. "You're not keeping your promise, Cinna," Augustus continued, "that you wouldn't interrupt me. Yes, you've undertaken to murder me, in such a place, on such a day, in such company, in such a manner." At those words, seeing Cinna struck dumb — not because of his promise but because his conscience had collapsed under the weight of the evidence — Augustus went on: "Now, to what end were you going to do it? To be emperor? Believe me, the Republic is in a sorry state if I'm the only man standing between you and the empire. You can't even defend your own household — only the other day you were beaten in a lawsuit by a mere freed slave's interest. Have you no means, no power anywhere except enough to take on Caesar? I'll step down from the throne if I'm the only obstacle to your hopes. Do you think the Paulli, the Fabii, the Cossii, the Servilii, and so many other noble Romans — noble not just in name but by the virtue that honours their nobility — would tolerate you?" After this, and a great deal more (he spoke for two long hours), he ended: "Now go, Cinna. Go. I give you the life I'd already given you once, when you were an enemy — and now I give it back to you again, traitor and parricide as you are. Let friendship begin between us from this moment, and let's see whether I have given, or you have received, your life with the better faith." And with that he left him. Some time later he advanced Cinna to the consulship, complaining that Cinna hadn't had the nerve to ask for it. He kept him afterwards as a very close friend, and was eventually made sole heir to his entire estate. Now — from the time of this episode, which befell Augustus in the fortieth year of his life, he never had another conspiracy or attempt made against him. He reaped the proper reward of his generous clemency. But things didn't go that way with our prince. His moderation and mercy did not protect him; he later fell into the net of a similar treason. So vain and futile a thing is human prudence; through all our projects, counsels, and precautions, Fortune will still be mistress of events.

Pompey’s nephew, of an illustrious family, who conspired to kill Augustus at sacrifice — and was told the whole plot back to his face, place, day and company, and then given his life a second time. He was made consul afterwards, was Augustus’s great friend, and left him his whole estate.

## modern-en · dion · 23:7

You'll read in history of many who, fearing for their lives, took the course of meeting and pre-empting conspiracies by punishment and revenge; but I find very few who got any advantage from this — witness so many Roman emperors. Whoever finds himself in such danger ought not to expect much from his vigilance or his power. For how hard a thing it is to secure oneself from an enemy hiding behind the face of the most devoted friend, or to read the wills and inner thoughts of those in our personal service. It does little good to have a guard of foreigners around you and to be always fenced in by armed men: whoever despises his own life is master of yours. And besides, this continual suspicion, which makes a prince mistrustful of all the world, must of necessity be a strange torment to him. That's why Dion, when warned that Callippus was watching for an opportunity to take his life, never had the heart to inquire more closely into it. He said he'd rather die than live in that misery — having to stand continually on guard, not just against his enemies but against his friends too. Alexander demonstrated the same point even more vividly and more roundly in action when, having been warned by a letter from Parmenio that his most beloved physician Philip had been bought with Darius' money to poison him, he handed Philip the letter to read and at the same moment drank off the potion Philip had brought him. Wasn't this to express a resolution that if his friends meant to send him out of the world, he was willing to give them the opportunity? Alexander is the supreme model for daring acts; but I don't know whether there's another passage in his life that shows such firm courage as this, or so illustrious an image of the beauty and greatness of his mind.

Warned that Callippus was watching for a chance to kill him, he would not inquire any further into it: he had rather die than live having to stand guard against his friends as well as his enemies.

## modern-en · duke-of-athens · 23:19

A stranger, having publicly said he could teach Dionysius, the tyrant of Syracuse, an infallible method for uncovering all the conspiracies his subjects could contrive against him, if Dionysius would pay him a good sum for his trouble, was sent for. Dionysius wanted to learn so necessary an art. The man answered that the only art he knew was this: Dionysius should give him a talent of silver and then boast that he'd received an unparalleled secret from him. Dionysius liked the trick, and accordingly had six hundred crowns counted out to him. It wasn't likely he'd give so large a sum to an unknown man except on account of some extraordinary disclosure, and the belief in this kept his enemies on edge. Princes, in fact, are wise to publicise the information they receive about plots against their lives, so as to convince people they have such good intelligence that nothing can be plotted against them without their getting wind of it instantly. The Duke of Athens did many foolish things in setting up his new tyranny over Florence, but one stood out above the rest: receiving the first intimation of a conspiracy the people were hatching against him from Matteo di Morozzo, one of the conspirators, he promptly put Morozzo to death — to suppress the rumour, so that no one would think any of his subjects disliked his government.

Who did a great many foolish things in setting up his tyranny over Florence, and this the most notable: told of the conspiracy by one of the conspirators, he put the informer to death at once, so that nobody should think the city disliked his government.

## modern-en · hercules · 24:7

And as for the philosophers — a sort of men remote from public affairs — they were also sometimes mocked, by the comic licence of their times, for opinions and manners that made them appear ridiculous to men of a different cast. Even if you were the fiftieth in descent from Hercules, they regard it as great vanity to set such a value on what is merely a gift of fortune. From whom, the philosophers say, you might be the fiftieth descendant and still have nothing but a gift of fortune to boast of.

## modern-en · crates · 24:11

As for the philosophers — as I said — if they were great in knowledge, they were even greater in action. Take the geometer of Syracuse: when he was disturbed at his contemplation to apply his skill to the defence of his country, he immediately set in motion dreadful and prodigious engines that produced effects beyond all human expectation. Yet he himself disdained all his handiwork, thinking that in this he had played the mere mechanic and violated the dignity of his art, of which these performances were only trivial experiments and playthings. So whenever the philosophers have been put to the test of action, they've been seen to rise to such a pitch that it's clear their souls were marvellously elevated and enriched by their knowledge. But some of them, seeing the reins of government in the hands of incompetent men, kept clear of all political administration. Crates, when asked how long it was necessary to philosophise, answered: "Until our armies are no longer commanded by fools." Heraclitus resigned the royalty to his brother; and to the Ephesians, who reproached him for spending his time playing with children before the temple, he said: "Isn't it better to do this than to sit at the helm of affairs in your company?" Others have raised their imagination above the world and fortune, and looked on the tribunals of justice, even the thrones of kings, as paltry and contemptible. Empedocles refused the royalty the Agrigentines offered him. Thales was once arguing against the trouble men take to grow rich, and someone in the company answered that he was like the fox who complained of what he couldn't reach. He had a mind, for the joke's sake, to show the contrary. He gathered up all his wits for the occasion, applied them wholly to profit and gain, set up a trading operation, and in one year brought in such great wealth that the most experienced merchants couldn't, in a whole lifetime of effort, have heaped together so much. As for what Aristotle reports of those who called him, Anaxagoras, and others of their profession wise but not prudent — for not applying their study to more profitable things — I don't really swallow that verbal distinction; nor does it serve to excuse my pedants, for if you look at the low and needy circumstances they're content with, the more reasonable verdict is that they are neither wise nor prudent.

Asked how long it was necessary to philosophise, he answered: till our armies are no more commanded by fools. He is also named to place his brother Pasicles, the philosopher who laid his hand in the wrong place in petitioning a great man.

## modern-en · lucullus · 24:23

We take other men's knowledge and opinions on trust — which is an idle, superficial sort of learning. We must make it our own. We're like the man who, needing fire, went to a neighbour's house to fetch some and, finding a very good one there, sat down to warm himself without remembering to carry any back with him. What good does it do us to have a stomach full of meat if it isn't digested, isn't incorporated into us, doesn't nourish and sustain us? Can we imagine that Lucullus, whom letters alone (without any experience) made so great a captain, learned to be so in that perfunctory way? We let ourselves lean so heavily on another man's arm that we destroy our own strength. Do I want to fortify myself against the fear of death? It must be at Seneca's expense. Do I want to extract some consolation for myself or my friend? I borrow it from Cicero. I could have found it in myself if I'd been trained to make use of my own reason. I don't like this dependent, mendicant understanding; for though we can become learned by other men's learning, a man can only be wise by his own wisdom:

Whom letters alone, without any experience, made so great a captain — and who did not learn it, Montaigne says, in the perfunctory way we learn.

## modern-en · protagoras · 24:33

These pedants of ours, as Plato says of the Sophists their cousins, are of all men the ones who most pretend to be useful to humanity, and yet alone of all men they not only fail to improve what is committed to them — as a carpenter or mason would — but make their charges worse, and make us pay them for making them worse into the bargain. If the rule Protagoras proposed to his pupils were followed — that they should either pay his asking price or swear an oath in the temple as to how much they reckoned the benefit they'd received under his tuition was worth, and pay him accordingly — my pedagogues would find themselves badly stuck if they had to be judged by the affidavits of my experience. My Perigord dialect very neatly calls these pretenders to learning lettre-ferits — letter-stamped, as if letters had been hammered onto them with a mallet. And in truth, for the most part, they appear to be deprived even of common sense. The farmer and the cobbler go simply and honestly about their business, speaking only of what they know and understand; but these fellows, in order to make a show and gain a reputation, parade about their ridiculous knowledge that floats on the surface of the brain, constantly tangling themselves up in their own nonsense. They speak fine words sometimes, true enough — let someone wiser apply them. They're wonderfully well acquainted with Galen, but not at all with the patient's disease; they'll already have deafened you with a long row of laws, while understanding nothing of the case in hand; they have the theory of everything — let who will put it into practice.

The sophist who let his pupils either pay his demand or swear in the temple what they thought the teaching had been worth — a rule under which, Montaigne says, his own pedagogues would be sorely gravelled.

## modern-en · adrian-turnebus · 24:37

Whoever closely examines and thoroughly sifts this sort of people, with whom the world is so pestered, will find, as I have done, that for the most part they understand neither others nor themselves; that their memories are full enough, but their judgment totally empty — with a few exceptions, men whom nature has of itself formed into better shape. I noticed this, for example, in Adrian Turnebus, who, having never professed anything but pure learning, and in that, in my opinion, the greatest man we've seen in a thousand years, had nothing of the pedant in him except the wearing of his gown and a little outward fashion that could never be civilised into courtier ways — which in themselves are nothing. I hate our people who can less easily endure an ill-cut robe than an ill-shaped mind, and who measure a man by the leg he makes, by his behaviour, even by the very fashion of his boots, to judge what kind of man he is. Within Turnebus, there wasn't a more polished soul on earth. I have often deliberately put him onto subjects far from his profession, and found such a clear insight, such a quick apprehension, such a solid judgment, that you'd have thought he'd practised nothing else but arms, and been employed all his life in affairs of state. These are great and vigorous natures,

The one man of pure learning Montaigne exempts from the charge of pedantry, and in his opinion the greatest of the last thousand years: nothing of the pedant about him but the gown, and within, not a more polished soul upon earth. Montaigne says he put him on arguments far outside his profession and found him as quick as if he had spent his life in arms or affairs of state.

And this, perhaps, is the reason why neither we nor theology require much learning in women. Francis, Duke of Brittany, son of John V, when someone was talking with him about his marriage to Isabella, daughter of the King of Scotland, and added that she was modestly bred and without any learning, answered that he liked her the better for it, and that a woman was wise enough if she could tell her husband's shirt from his doublet. It is a thing worth great consideration, that in the excellent — indeed, for its perfection, prodigious — civil regime laid down by Lycurgus, though so concerned for the education of children as the matter of greatest importance, even at the very seat of the Muses, he makes so little mention of learning, as if that high-spirited youth, disdaining all other subjection but that of virtue, ought to be supplied not with tutors to read them arts and sciences, but with masters who would only instruct them in valour, prudence, and justice — an example Plato followed in his Laws. Their method of discipline was to put questions to the boys about judgments on men and their actions; if the boys praised or condemned this or that person or deed, they had to give a reason for so doing, and by this means they sharpened their understanding and learned what was right. Astyages, in Xenophon, asks Cyrus to give an account of his last lesson, and the lesson went like this: "A big boy in our school, having a short little jacket, took by force a longer one from another boy who wasn't as tall as he was, and gave him his own in exchange. I, being appointed judge of the dispute, ruled that each should keep the coat he had, because each was now better fitted with the other's than with his own. Whereupon my master told me I'd done badly: I had only considered the fit of the garments, when I ought to have considered the justice of the thing, which required that nothing be forcibly taken from anyone that was rightfully his." ## modern-en · antipater · 24:61

They used to go, it's said, to the other cities of Greece to look for rhetoricians, painters, and musicians; but to Lacedaemon for legislators, magistrates, and generals. At Athens you learned to speak well; here, to do well. Those people cudgelled their brains about words; these made it their business to inquire into things. There was an endless babbling of the tongue; here, a continual exercise of the soul. ## modern-en · tamerlane · 24:63

Examples have shown us that in military affairs, and all others of that active sort, the study of the sciences softens and saps men's courage rather than strengthening and exciting it. The most powerful empire in the world today is that of the Turks — a people equally trained in the esteem of arms and the contempt of letters. I find Rome was more warlike before she grew so learned. The most warlike nations now in existence are the most rude and ignorant: the Scythians, the Parthians, Tamerlane — proof enough. When the Goths overran Greece, the only thing that preserved the libraries from the fire was that someone convinced them to leave this kind of furniture untouched for the enemy, as the surest way to divert them from arms and fix them in a lazy, sedentary life. When our King Charles VIII found himself master of the kingdom of Naples and a good part of Tuscany almost without striking a blow, the nobles around him put this unexpected ease of conquest down to this: the princes and nobles of Italy were more concerned to make themselves clever and learned than vigorous and warlike.

I never seriously settled down to read any book of solid learning except Plutarch and Seneca; and there, like the Danaids, I'm forever filling and forever leaking; something of it drips onto this paper, but little or nothing stays with me. History is my particular game where reading is concerned, or else poetry, for which I have a particular fondness and esteem. For as Cleanthes said, just as the voice, forced through the narrow throat of a trumpet, comes out sharper and more forceful, so a sentence pressed within the harmony of verse seems to me to dart out more briskly upon the understanding, and strikes my ear and apprehension with a smarter and more pleasing effect. As for the natural parts I have, of which this is the test, I find them bowing under the burden. My fancy and judgment only grope in the dark, tripping and stumbling on the way; and when I've gone as far as I can, I'm in no way satisfied. I still see a new and greater extent of land before me, with a troubled and imperfect sight, wrapped up in clouds I can't penetrate. And as I take it upon myself to write indifferently about whatever comes into my head, using nothing but my own natural means, if I happen to meet, in some good author (as often happens), the same topics I've attempted to write upon — as just now, in Plutarch's "Of the Force of Imagination" — to see myself so weak, so faint, so heavy and flat, in comparison with those better writers, I both pity and despise myself. Yet I take some pleasure in this, that my opinions often have the honour and good fortune to coincide with theirs, that I'm travelling in the same path, though at a very great distance, and can say, "Ah, that is so." I'm further satisfied to find I have one quality that not everyone is blessed with: the ability to see the vast difference between them and me. And in spite of all that, I let my own inventions, low and feeble as they are, run on in their course, without mending or papering over the defects this comparison has laid bare to my view. To be honest, a man needs a strong back to keep pace with such people. The indiscreet scribblers of our times, who among their laborious nothings insert whole sections and pages from ancient authors, hoping by that means to lend lustre to their own writings, do quite the opposite; for the infinite contrast between the ornaments and their own composition makes their own work look so sallow and deformed that they lose much more than they gain.

Who eternally fill and whose vessels eternally run out — Montaigne’s figure for his own reading of Plutarch and Seneca. The modern edition spells them Danaids.

## modern-en · apollodorus · 25:3

The philosophers Chrysippus and Epicurus were of two entirely opposite tempers in this: the first not only mixed passages and sayings from other authors into his books, but entire pieces — in one, the whole Medea of Euripides — which gave Apollodorus occasion to say that if a man picked out of his writings everything that was not his, he'd be left with blank paper. Epicurus, on the contrary, in the three hundred volumes he left behind, has not so much as one quotation.

Who said that if a man picked out of Chrysippus’s writings everything that was none of his, he would leave him nothing but blank paper. Not the Apollodorus whose heart spoke to him in the dream of being flayed and boiled.

## modern-en · capilupus · 25:4

The other day I happened to come across this piece of luck. I was reading a French book where, after long wandering through a great many words so dull, so insipid, so void of wit or common sense that they were really only French words, after a long and tedious slog I came at last to a passage that was lofty, rich, and lifted to the very clouds. Had I found either a gentle slope or a gradual ascent up to it, there'd have been some excuse; but it was so sheer a precipice, so wholly cut off from the rest of the work, that by the first six words I found myself flying off into another world, and from there saw the vale I had climbed out of as so deep and low that I've never had the heart to descend into it again. If I set out one of my discourses with such rich spoils, it would too clearly expose the imperfection of my own writing. To rebuke in others the fault I'm guilty of myself seems to me no more unreasonable than condemning (as I often do) in myself the faults of others; they should be reproved everywhere and given no sanctuary. I know perfectly well how brazenly I try, at every turn, to equal myself to my thefts, to make my style march hand in hand with them, not without an audacious hope of deceiving my reader's eye. But it's as much by the benefit of my application that I hope to do it as by my invention or any force of my own. Besides, I don't pretend to fight the whole body of these champions, nor hand to hand with any single one of them; it's only by skirmishes and light feints that I engage them. I don't grapple with them — I only try their strength, and never push so far as I pretend. If I could hold them in play, I'd be a brave fellow indeed, for I only attack them where they are most sinewy and strong. To cover yourself (as I've seen some do) with another man's armour, so that even your fingertips don't show; to carry on a project (as anyone with a touch of the scholar can do on an ordinary subject) under old inventions patched up here and there with your own scraps, and then to try to conceal the theft and pass it off as your own — that's first an injustice and meanness of spirit in those who do it; since they have nothing of their own fit to win them a reputation, they try to do it by foisting on the world things that aren't theirs at all in their own name. And then it's a ridiculous folly to content yourself with the ignorant approval of the common sort by such a pitiful trick, at the same time degrading yourself in the eyes of men of understanding, who turn up their noses at all that borrowed plaster, even though their praise alone is worth having. For my own part, there's nothing I'd less willingly do; nor have I said so much about others except to get a better chance to explain myself. Nor do I aim, in this, at the composers of centos who openly declare themselves such — of which I've known several very ingenious in my time, particularly one writing under the name of Capilupus, besides the ancients. These are really men of wit, and they make it clear they are, both in that way and in others — as for example Lipsius, in that learned and laborious tissue of his Politics.

A composer of centos Montaigne knew of, and one of the writers he exempts from the charge of stitching other men’s work into their own under their own name — because such men declare themselves for what they are.

## modern-en · cimon · 25:7

Now, madam, if I had any competence on this subject, I couldn't employ it better than by offering my best instructions to the little man who threatens you shortly with a happy birth — for you are too generous to begin otherwise than with a male. Having had so great a hand in arranging your marriage, I have a particular interest in the greatness and prosperity of whatever issue comes from it; besides which, your long possession of my service obliges me to wish honour and advantage to everything that concerns you. But in truth, all I understand about this is that the greatest and most important difficulty of human knowledge is the education of children. For as in agriculture the husbandry preceding planting, and the planting itself, is straightforward and well known, but once what is planted comes alive there's a great deal more to be done, more art, more care, more difficulty in cultivating and bringing it to perfection — so it is with men. It's no hard matter to get children; but once they're born, the trouble, anxiety, and care of training, instructing, and bringing them up begins. The signs of their inclinations at that tender age are so obscure, and the promises so uncertain and deceptive, that it's very hard to build any solid judgment or conjecture on them. Look at Cimon, for instance, and Themistocles, and a thousand others, who much disappointed the expectations people had of them. Cubs of bears and puppies readily reveal their natural disposition; but men, as soon as they grow up, settling into certain habits, taking on certain opinions, conforming to particular laws and customs, easily change — or at least disguise — their true and real character. And yet it's hard to force the bent of nature. So, for not having chosen the right course, we often take great pains and waste a good part of our time training up children for things they are by nature totally unfit for. In this difficulty, all the same, I'm clearly of the opinion that they ought to be brought up in the best and most useful studies, without taking too much notice of, or being too superstitious about, the slight prognostics they give of themselves in their tender years — to which Plato, in his Republic, gives, it seems to me, too much weight.

With Themistocles, one of the thousand men who very much deceived the expectation others had of them — Montaigne’s warning against reading a child’s promise too early. It is he who besieged Boges in Eion and offered him a safe return into Asia with all his wealth.

Madam, science is a great ornament and a thing of marvellous use, especially for persons raised to the rank of fortune you are. In truth, in people of mean and low condition it can't perform its true office; for its natural inclination is to assist in the conduct of war, in the government of peoples, in negotiating the leagues and friendships of princes and foreign nations, rather than in framing a syllogism in logic, pleading a case in law, or prescribing a dose of pills in medicine. So, madam, since I'm sure you won't omit so necessary a feature in the education of your children — you yourself having tasted its sweetness, being of a learned line (we still have the writings of the ancient Counts of Foix, from whom your husband and yourself are both descended; and Monsieur de Candale, your uncle, daily obliges the world with more, which will extend the reputation of this quality in your family for many ages to come) — I'll take this occasion to share with you one particular fancy of my own, contrary to the common method, which is all I can contribute to your service in this matter.

Diane de Foix’s uncle, who every day obliges the world with writings of his own.

## modern-en · arcesilaus · 25:11

It's the custom of teachers to be eternally booming into their pupil's ears, as if pouring through a funnel, while the pupil's only business is to repeat what they've said. I want a tutor to correct this error, and right from the start, according to the capacity he has to deal with, to put it to the test — letting his pupil taste things himself, and discover and choose for himself, sometimes opening the way for him, sometimes leaving him to open it on his own. That is, I don't want the tutor alone to invent and speak; he should also hear his pupil speak in turn. Socrates, and after him Arcesilaus, first made their pupils speak, and then they spoke to them.

Who, like Socrates before him, made his scholars speak first and then spoke to them — and whom pure wine despatched as it did Stilpo, though in his case not by design.

## modern-en · epicharmus · 25:25

Let him at least know that he knows. He'll need to drink in their knowledge, but not be poisoned by their precepts; and no matter if he forgets where he got his learning, provided he knows how to apply it to his own use. Truth and reason are common to everyone, and belong no more to the one who spoke them first than to the one who speaks them after; it's no more according to Plato than according to me, since both he and I equally see and understand them. Bees cull their various sweets from this flower and that blossom, here and there where they find them, but afterwards they themselves make the honey, which is all and purely their own — no more thyme and marjoram. In the same way, the boy will transform and shuffle together the fragments he borrows from others, to compile a work absolutely his own — that is, his judgment. His instruction, labour, and study aim at nothing else but to form that. He's not obliged to disclose where he got the materials that helped him, but only to show what he himself has done with them. Men who live by pillage and borrowing display their purchases and their buildings to every passer-by; they don't broadcast how they got the money. We don't see a lawyer's fees and perquisites; we see the alliances he uses to fortify himself and his family, and the titles and honours he's secured. No man advertises his income, or at least how it comes in, but everyone publishes his acquisitions. The advantages of our study are to become better and wiser. As Epicharmus says, it's the understanding that sees and hears, the understanding that improves everything, that orders everything, that acts, rules, and reigns; all the other faculties are blind, and deaf, and without soul. And we certainly render it timid and servile by not allowing it the liberty to do anything of itself. Who ever asked his pupil what he thought of grammar and rhetoric, or of such-and-such a sentence of Cicero? Our masters stick them, fully feathered, into our memories, where they're set up like oracles, the letters and syllables themselves treated as the substance of the thing. To know by rote is not to know; it just means to retain what one has entrusted to memory. What a man truly knows and understands he disposes of freely, without reference to the author he got it from or fumbling through the pages of his book. A merely bookish learning is a poor, paltry kind of learning; it may serve for decoration, but it provides no foundation for any structure to be built on it — according to Plato, who says that constancy, faith, and sincerity are the true philosophy, and the other sciences, directed to other ends, are only counterfeit paint. I could wish that Paluel or Pompey, those two famous dancers of my time, could have taught us to cut capers just by watching them, without our stirring from our seats — as these men pretend to inform the understanding without ever setting it to work. Or that we could learn to ride, handle a pike, play the lute, or sing without the trouble of practice, as these try to teach us to judge and speak well without exercising us in judging or speaking. Now in the start of our studies, and in their progress, whatever presents itself to us is book enough: a roguish trick of a page, a stupid mistake of a servant, a joke at the table — all are fresh subjects.

Who said it is the understanding that sees and hears, the understanding that orders and rules everything, and that all the other faculties are blind and deaf and without soul.

## modern-en · signora-livia · 25:26

And for this reason, conversation with men is very useful, and so is travel into foreign countries — not to bring back (as most of our young gentlemen do) an account of how many paces around Santa Rotonda is, or the richness of Signora Livia's petticoats, or, as some others, how much Nero's face in some statue in some old ruin is longer or broader than the one on some medal; but mainly to bring back an account of the humours, manners, customs, and laws of the nations where he's been, and so that we may whet and sharpen our wits by rubbing them against those of others. I would have a boy sent abroad very young — and first, to kill two birds with one stone, into those neighbouring nations whose language is most different from our own, and to which, if the tongue isn't shaped early, it grows too stiff to bend.

Whose petticoats are one of the things Montaigne says a young traveller ought not to come home able to describe. Not the Livia who was Augustus’s wife.

## modern-en · marcellus · 25:51

In this conversation with men, I mean also, and chiefly, those who only live in the records of history: by reading those books, he'll converse with the great and heroic souls of the best ages. It's an idle, vain study for those who treat it negligently; but for those who do it with care and observation, it's a study of incalculable value — and the only study, as Plato reports, that the Lacedaemonians reserved for themselves. What profit will he not reap, as to the business of men, by reading Plutarch's Lives! But let my governor remember what end his instructions are mainly directed at, and not so much impress on his pupil's memory the date of Carthage's fall as the manners of Hannibal and Scipio, nor so much where Marcellus died as why it was unworthy of his duty that he died there. Let him not teach him so much the narrative parts of history as how to judge them. The reading of history, in my opinion, is something we apply ourselves to with the most varying degrees of attention. I have read a hundred things in Livy that another has not, or not noticed at least; and Plutarch has read a hundred things there that I never could find, or perhaps that the author never wrote. To some it's merely a grammar exercise; to others the very anatomy of philosophy, by which the most abstruse parts of our human nature are reached. There are in Plutarch many long discourses very worth reading and observing carefully — he is, in my view, of all writers the greatest master in that kind of writing — but there are a thousand others he has only touched and glanced at, where he only points his finger to show us which way we may go if we will, and contents himself with sometimes giving us one brisk hit on the trickiest point of the question, from which we must grope out the rest for ourselves. Take, for example, his saying that the inhabitants of Asia came to be vassals of one man because they couldn't pronounce one syllable, which is "No." That saying perhaps gave La Boétie the matter and occasion to write his "Voluntary Servitude." Just to see him pick out a slight action in a man's life, or a mere word that hardly seems to amount even to that, is itself a whole discourse. It's to our prejudice that men of understanding should so immoderately affect brevity; no doubt their reputation is the better for it, but in the meantime we are the worse for it. Plutarch had rather we should applaud his judgment than commend his knowledge; he had rather leave us with an appetite to read more than glutted with what we've read already. He knew very well that one may say too much even on the best subjects, and that Alexandridas justly reproached someone who made very good but too long speeches to the Ephori, saying: "O stranger! you speak the things you should speak, but not as you should speak them." Those who have lean, spare bodies stuff themselves out with clothes; so those who are short on substance try to make up for it with words.

Whose death, Montaigne says, the pupil should be taught to judge rather than to locate: not so much where he died as why it was unworthy of his duty that he died there.

All singularity in our manners and conditions is to be avoided, as inconsistent with civil society. Who wouldn't be astonished at so strange a constitution as that of Demophoön, steward to Alexander the Great, who sweated in the shade and shivered in the sun? I've seen people who fled the smell of a ripe apple more swiftly than from the shot of a harquebus; others afraid of a mouse; others who threw up at the sight of cream; others ready to faint at the making of a feather bed; Germanicus could endure neither the sight nor the crowing of a cock. I won't deny there may, perhaps, be some hidden cause and natural aversion in these cases; but in my opinion a man could overcome it, if he took it in time. Precept has worked so effectively on me, though not without some effort, I confess, that, beer excepted, my appetite accommodates itself indifferently to all sorts of food. Young bodies are supple; one should therefore at that age bend and shape them to all fashions and customs. And provided one can keep the appetite and the will within their due limits, let a young man, in God's name, be made fit for all nations and all companies, even for debauchery and excess if need be — that is, where he does it in compliance with the customs of the place. Let him be able to do anything, but love to do nothing but what is good. The philosophers themselves don't justify Callisthenes for forfeiting his master Alexander's favour by refusing to pledge him a cup of wine. Let him laugh, play, drink, even wench with his prince. Indeed I'd have him, even in his debauches, outdo the rest of the company, and excel his companions in ability and stamina — and that he may not stop doing it for want of power or knowledge how, but only for want of will.

Alexander the Great’s steward, who sweated in the shade and shivered in the sun. The modern edition spells him Demophoön.

Let our pupil only be well furnished with things, and words will follow fast enough; he'll pull them after him if they don't come voluntarily. I've heard people make excuses that they can't express themselves, pretending to have their minds full of a great many fine things which, for lack of eloquence, they can't bring out. It's a mere pretext, nothing else. Do you want to know what I think of it? I think they're nothing but shadows of some imperfect images and conceptions they don't know what to make of, and consequently can't bring out. They don't yet understand themselves what they're trying to say, and if you just watch how they haggle and stammer on the verge of delivery, you'll soon conclude that their labour is not in giving birth but in conception — that they're still licking their formless embryo. For my part I hold, and Socrates lays it down, that whoever has a sprightly and clear conception in his mind will express it well enough in one language or another, and, if he's mute, by signs.

At the head of the troop of horse behind the two pedants on the road to Orleans — one of whom, asked who the gentleman was, and thinking his companion meant, answered that he was no gentleman but a grammarian, and that he himself was a logician.

## modern-en · aper · 25:117

He knows nothing of ablative, conjunctive, substantive, or grammar — no more than his footman, or a fishwife on the Petit Pont — and yet they'll give you a bellyful of talk if you'll listen, and perhaps stumble as little in their language as the best masters of art in France. He knows no rhetoric, no way of buttering up the gentle reader with a preface; and he doesn't care to know it. All this fine paint is easily rubbed off by the lustre of a simple and blunt truth; these flourishes only serve to amuse the common sort, who can't take in more solid and nourishing diet, as Aper very evidently shows in Tacitus. The ambassadors of Samos, having prepared a long and elegant oration, came to Cleomenes, king of Sparta, to incite him to war against the tyrant Polycrates. After listening to their speech with great gravity and patience, he gave them this answer: "As for the exordium, I don't remember it, nor consequently the middle of your speech; and as to the conclusion, I won't do what you ask." A very neat answer, I think, and a pack of learned orators very sweetly stuck. And what about the other man? The Athenians were to choose one of two architects for a very great building they had designed. The first, a pert affected fellow, offered his services in a long premeditated discourse on the subject of the work, and by his eloquence won the votes of the people. But the other said only three words: "Athenians, what this man says, I will do." When Cicero was in the heat and flow of an eloquent harangue, many were struck with admiration; but Cato only laughed, saying, "We have a comical consul." Let it come before or after, a good sentence, or something well said, is always in season; if it doesn't fit well with what went before, nor cohere much with what follows, it's good in itself. I'm not one of those who think that good rhyme makes a good poem. Let a man make short long and long short if he likes — it's no great matter; if there's invention, and if the wit and judgment have done their work, I'll say, "There's a good poet, but a poor rhymer."

Who demonstrates in Tacitus how easily the fine decoration of painted speech is effaced by the lustre of a simple and blunt truth.

— rather hard than wearisome; free from affectation; irregular, broken, and bold; where every piece makes up an entire body; not like a pedant, a preacher, or a pleader, but rather a soldierly style, as Suetonius calls that of Julius Caesar — though I see no reason why he should call it that. ## modern-en · aristophanes-grammarian · 25:143

That eloquence prejudices the subject it would advance, which wholly draws us to itself. And as it's a ridiculous effeminacy in our outward dress to distinguish ourselves by an odd, unusual fashion, so in language to study new phrases and affect words not in common use comes from a puerile and scholastic ambition. May I be bound to speak no other language than what is spoken in the markets of Paris! Aristophanes the grammarian was quite wrong to scold Epicurus for his plain way of delivering himself, his only aim being clarity of speech. The imitation of words, by its own ease, immediately spreads through a whole people; but the imitation of inventing and properly applying those words is much slower. The general sort of readers, having found a similar robe, mistakenly imagine they have the same body and inside too — whereas force and sinew can never be borrowed; the gloss and outward ornament, that is, words and elocution, can. Most of those I talk with speak the same language I write here, but whether they think the same thoughts I can't say. The Athenians, says Plato, study fullness and elegance of speech; the Lacedaemonians prize brevity; and those of Crete aim more at fecundity of conception than fertility of speech — and these last are the best. Zeno used to say he had two sorts of disciples: one he called philological, eager to learn things, and these were his favourites; the others, logophilic, who cared for nothing but words. Not that fine speaking isn't a very good and praiseworthy quality; but it's not so excellent and so necessary as some would make it; and I'm scandalised that our whole life should be spent in nothing else. I would first understand my own language, and that of my neighbours, with whom most of my business and conversation lies.

Who was quite out, Montaigne says, in reproving Epicurus for his plain way of delivering himself and for an oratory whose whole design was to be understood.

## modern-en · nicolas-grouchy · 25:144

No doubt Greek and Latin are very great ornaments, and of very great use; but we buy them too dear. I'll set out one way, tried on my own person, by which they can be had cheaper, and anyone who wants to may make use of it. My late father, having made the most precise inquiries any man could make among men of the greatest learning and judgment for an exact method of education, was warned by them of the inconvenience then in use, and made to believe that the tedious time we spent learning the tongues of men who had them for nothing was the sole cause we couldn't reach the greatness of soul and perfection of knowledge of the ancient Greeks and Romans. I don't, however, believe that to be the only cause. So it was, that my father's expedient was this: in my infancy, before I began to speak, he committed me to the care of a German, who later died a famous physician in France, totally ignorant of our language and very fluent and a great critic in Latin. This man, whom he had fetched out of his own country and engaged with a great salary for this one purpose, had me continually with him. He had two others of lesser learning joined to him, to attend me and relieve him; they spoke to me in no language but Latin. As to the rest of the household, it was an inviolable rule that neither my father, nor my mother, nor any valet or chambermaid spoke anything in my presence but the few Latin words each had learned to gabble with me. It's not to be imagined what an advantage this proved for the whole family: my father and mother by this means learned enough Latin to understand it perfectly and to speak it well enough for any necessary use; so did those of the servants who were most often with me. In short, we Latined it at such a rate that it overflowed to all the neighbouring villages, where there still remain, established by custom, several Latin names of artisans and their tools. As for myself, I was over six years old before I understood any more French or Perigord dialect than Arabic; and without art, books, grammar, precept, whipping, or the cost of a tear, I had by that age learned to speak Latin as pure as my master's, since I had no means of mixing it with anything else. If, for example, they were to give me a theme in the college fashion, they gave it to the others in French, but to me they had to give it in bad Latin, to turn it into good. And Nicolas Grouchy, who wrote a book De Comitiis Romanorum; Guillaume Guérente, who wrote a commentary on Aristotle; George Buchanan, that great Scottish poet; and Marc-Antoine Muret (whom France and Italy have both acknowledged as the best orator of his time), my domestic tutors, all of them often told me that I had in my infancy that language so fluent and ready that they were afraid to enter into conversation with me. Buchanan in particular, whom I later saw in attendance on the late Mareschal de Brissac, then told me he was about to write a treatise on education, the example for which he intended to take from mine — for he was then tutor to that Comte de Brissac who afterwards proved so brave and valiant a gentleman.

Who wrote De Comitiis Romanorum, and one of the domestic tutors who told Montaigne that his infant Latin was so fluent they were afraid to enter into discourse with him.

In short, we Latined it at such a rate that it overflowed to all the neighbouring villages, where there still remain, established by custom, several Latin names of artisans and their tools. As for myself, I was over six years old before I understood any more French or Perigord dialect than Arabic; and without art, books, grammar, precept, whipping, or the cost of a tear, I had by that age learned to speak Latin as pure as my master's, since I had no means of mixing it with anything else. If, for example, they were to give me a theme in the college fashion, they gave it to the others in French, but to me they had to give it in bad Latin, to turn it into good. And Nicolas Grouchy, who wrote a book De Comitiis Romanorum; Guillaume Guérente, who wrote a commentary on Aristotle; George Buchanan, that great Scottish poet; and Marc-Antoine Muret (whom France and Italy have both acknowledged as the best orator of his time), my domestic tutors, all of them often told me that I had in my infancy that language so fluent and ready that they were afraid to enter into conversation with me. Buchanan in particular, whom I later saw in attendance on the late Mareschal de Brissac, then told me he was about to write a treatise on education, the example for which he intended to take from mine — for he was then tutor to that Comte de Brissac who afterwards proved so brave and valiant a gentleman.

Buchanan’s pupil, who afterwards proved so valiant and brave a gentleman.

## modern-en · counts-of-foix · 25:8

Madam, science is a great ornament and a thing of marvellous use, especially for persons raised to the rank of fortune you are. In truth, in people of mean and low condition it can't perform its true office; for its natural inclination is to assist in the conduct of war, in the government of peoples, in negotiating the leagues and friendships of princes and foreign nations, rather than in framing a syllogism in logic, pleading a case in law, or prescribing a dose of pills in medicine. So, madam, since I'm sure you won't omit so necessary a feature in the education of your children — you yourself having tasted its sweetness, being of a learned line (we still have the writings of the ancient Counts of Foix, from whom your husband and yourself are both descended; and Monsieur de Candale, your uncle, daily obliges the world with more, which will extend the reputation of this quality in your family for many ages to come) — I'll take this occasion to share with you one particular fancy of my own, contrary to the common method, which is all I can contribute to your service in this matter.

The house Diane de Foix and her husband are both descended from, and whose writings Montaigne cites as evidence that learning runs in the family.

## modern-en · the-graces · 25:90

For the rest, this method of education should be carried on with a stern sweetness, quite contrary to the practice of our pedants, who, instead of tempting and luring children into letters by apt and gentle means, present nothing in fact but rods and ferules, horror and cruelty. Away with this violence! Away with this compulsion! Nothing, I'm convinced, more dulls and degenerates a well-born nature. If you would have him fear shame and chastisement, don't harden him to them. Inure him to heat and cold, to wind and sun, and to dangers he ought to despise; wean him from all effeminacy and delicacy in clothes and lodging, eating and drinking; accustom him to everything, so he may not be a Sir Paris, a carpet-knight, but a sinewy, hardy, vigorous young man. From childhood to my present age I've been of this opinion, and I'm still of it. But among other things, the strict regime of most of our colleges has always displeased me; they could perhaps have erred less harmfully on the indulgent side. It's a real house of correction for imprisoned youth. They're made debauched by being punished before they've done anything to deserve it. Just walk in when they're at their lessons and you'll hear nothing but the cries of boys being beaten and the thunder of pedagogues drunk with fury. A pretty way that, to lure these tender and timorous souls to love their books — with a furious face and a rod in hand! A cursed and pernicious method! Besides what Quintilian has very well observed, that this imperious authority is often followed by very dangerous consequences, and particularly our way of chastising. How much more decent would it be to see their classrooms strewn with green leaves and fine flowers than with the bloody stumps of birch and willow! If it were left to me, I'd paint the school with pictures of joy and gladness, Flora and the Graces, as the philosopher Speusippus did his. Where their profit is, let them also have their pleasure. The food that's proper and wholesome for children should be sweetened with sugar, and what's dangerous to them embittered with gall. It's marvellous to see how careful Plato is in his Laws about the gaiety and diversions of the youth of his city, and how much and how often he expatiates on the races, sports, songs, leaps, and dances — of which, he says, antiquity gave the ordering and patronage specifically to the gods themselves, to Apollo, Minerva, and the Muses. He goes on at length and is very particular in giving countless precepts for exercises; but as for the lettered sciences, he says very little, and only seems to recommend poetry on account of music.

With Flora, the figures Speusippus painted his school with.

## modern-en · plautus · 25:146

The first taste I had for books came to me from the pleasure of reading the fables of Ovid's Metamorphoses; for at about seven or eight I gave up all other diversions to read them, both because this was my native language, the easiest book I was acquainted with, and because of the subject, the most suited to my age. As for Lancelot of the Lake, Amadis of Gaul, Huon of Bordeaux, and such farragoes, by which children are most delighted, I had never so much as heard their names — nor do I yet know what they contain; so strict was the discipline I was raised in. But this was enough to make me neglect the other lessons prescribed me; and there I was infinitely lucky to have to do with an understanding tutor, who knew very well how to discreetly turn a blind eye to this and other little truancies of the same nature. By this means I ran through Virgil's Aeneid, then Terence, then Plautus, then some Italian comedies, lured by the sweetness of the subject; whereas if he had been so foolish as to break me off this diversion, I really believe I'd have brought away from college nothing but a hatred of books, as almost all our young gentlemen do. But he managed the business very tactfully, seeming to take no notice, and allowing me only such time as I could steal from my regular studies — which whetted my appetite to devour those books. For the chief things my father expected from those to whom he'd entrusted my education were affability and good humour; and to tell the truth, my manners had no vice but sloth and want of mettle. The fear wasn't that I'd do ill, but that I'd do nothing; no one predicted I'd be wicked, only useless; they foresaw idleness, not malice; and it's turned out accordingly. The complaints I hear of myself are these: "He's idle, cold in the offices of friendship and family, and in public matters too detached, too disdainful." But the most pointed of them don't say, "Why has he taken such-and-such? Why hasn't he paid so-and-so?" but, "Why doesn't he part with anything? Why doesn't he give?" And I'd take it as a favour if men would expect no greater works of supererogation from me than these. But they're unjust to demand from me what I don't owe, far more rigorously than they require from others what they do owe. In condemning me to that, they spoil the gratification of the act and deprive me of the gratitude that would be my due for it; whereas the active doing of good ought to have greater value coming from my hands, since I've never been on the receiving end at all. I can dispose all the more freely of my fortune the more it is mine, and of myself the more I am my own. And yet, if I were good at making my own case, I might quite easily turn aside these reproaches and let some people understand they aren't so much offended that I don't do enough, as that I'm able to do a great deal more than I do.

The Latin comic poet, one of the books the boy Montaigne ran through by stealth after Ovid and Terence, allured by the sweetness of the subject.

## modern-en · andreas-goveanus · 25:150

— I played the chief parts in the Latin tragedies of Buchanan, Guérente, and Muret, that were performed in our College of Guienne with great dignity. It's an exercise I don't disapprove of in young people of quality; and I've since seen our princes, after the example of some of the ancients, in person handsomely and commendably perform these exercises; it was even permitted to persons of quality to make a profession of it in Greece.

Principal of the College of Guienne, and without comparison the best man in that employment in France.
