## modern-en · chilo · 26:17

It is the novelty, more than the size, of things that tempts us to inquire into their causes. We ought to judge nature's infinite power with more reverence, and with a fuller acknowledgment of our own ignorance and weakness. How many unlikely things are testified to by people worthy of belief? Even if we cannot bring ourselves to accept them outright, we should at least suspend judgment, for to condemn them as impossible is, by a rash presumption, to claim that we know the outer limits of what is possible. If we properly understood the difference between the impossible and the unusual — and between what runs against the order of nature and what runs against common opinion — we would obey Chilo's rule of "Ne quid nimis": neither believe too quickly nor too slowly.

Who enjoined the rule Ne quid nimis — nothing too much — and who said: love him as if you were one day to hate him, and hate him as if you were one day to love him.

## modern-en · froissart · 26:18

When we read in Froissart that the Comte de Foix in Béarn knew, the day after, of the defeat of John, King of Castile, at Aljubarrota — and by what means he tells us he knew — we may be allowed a smile; the same for what our annals report about Pope Honorius performing the public obsequies of King Philip Augustus at Rome on the very day he died at Mantes, and ordering the like throughout Italy. These witnesses are perhaps not authoritative enough to bind us. But what about Plutarch, who, besides several examples drawn from antiquity, tells us that he himself knows for certain that under Domitian the news of Antony's defeat in Germany was published at Rome — many days' travel away — and spread through the whole world on the same day as the battle? And what about Caesar's opinion that the report often outruns the event itself? Shall we say that these careful men let themselves be taken in by the common run, because they were less clear-sighted than we are? Is there anything more delicate, more lucid, more lively than Pliny's judgment when he chooses to put it to work? Anything less affected? Leaving aside his learning, of which I make less account — in which of these qualities do any of us match him? And yet there is hardly a young schoolboy who does not catch him in untruth and pretend to set him right about the workings of nature. When we read in Bouchet the miracles wrought by the relics of St. Hilary, away with them: his standing is not enough to take from us the right to contradict him. But to condemn all such stories wholesale, out of hand, strikes me as a singular impudence. The great St. Augustine testifies that he saw a blind child recover sight at the relics of St. Gervasius and St. Protasius at Milan; a woman at Carthage cured of cancer by the sign of the cross made over her by a newly baptised woman; his close friend Hesperius driving the spirits out of his haunted house with a little earth from Our Lord's sepulchre, which earth, carried into the church, suddenly cured a paralytic; and a woman in a procession who, having touched St. Stephen's shrine with a nosegay and then rubbed her eyes with it, recovered her sight after years of blindness — among other miracles he claims to have seen with his own eyes. How do we excuse him, and the two holy bishops Aurelius and Maximinus, both of whom he names as witnesses? Are they ignorant, simple, credulous? Or malicious impostors? Is any man alive impudent enough to think himself the equal of these men in virtue, piety, learning, judgment, or any sort of perfection?

In whom Montaigne finds the Comte de Foix knowing in Bearn, the day after it happened, the defeat of John of Castile.

But what about Plutarch, who, besides several examples drawn from antiquity, tells us that he himself knows for certain that under Domitian the news of Antony's defeat in Germany was published at Rome — many days' travel away — and spread through the whole world on the same day as the battle? And what about Caesar's opinion that the report often outruns the event itself? Shall we say that these careful men let themselves be taken in by the common run, because they were less clear-sighted than we are? Is there anything more delicate, more lucid, more lively than Pliny's judgment when he chooses to put it to work? Anything less affected? Leaving aside his learning, of which I make less account — in which of these qualities do any of us match him? And yet there is hardly a young schoolboy who does not catch him in untruth and pretend to set him right about the workings of nature. When we read in Bouchet the miracles wrought by the relics of St. Hilary, away with them: his standing is not enough to take from us the right to contradict him. But to condemn all such stories wholesale, out of hand, strikes me as a singular impudence. The great St. Augustine testifies that he saw a blind child recover sight at the relics of St. Gervasius and St. Protasius at Milan; a woman at Carthage cured of cancer by the sign of the cross made over her by a newly baptised woman; his close friend Hesperius driving the spirits out of his haunted house with a little earth from Our Lord's sepulchre, which earth, carried into the church, suddenly cured a paralytic; and a woman in a procession who, having touched St. Stephen's shrine with a nosegay and then rubbed her eyes with it, recovered her sight after years of blindness — among other miracles he claims to have seen with his own eyes. How do we excuse him, and the two holy bishops Aurelius and Maximinus, both of whom he names as witnesses? Are they ignorant, simple, credulous? Or malicious impostors? Is any man alive impudent enough to think himself the equal of these men in virtue, piety, learning, judgment, or any sort of perfection?

Bishop of Poictiers and the famous enemy of the Arian heresy, whose relics Bouchet records the miracles of. Hearing in Syria that his only daughter Abra was being sought in marriage, he wrote telling her to put worldly pleasures aside for a greater husband — and then prayed without ceasing that God would take her out of the world, which soon happened, to his singular joy. His wife, hearing how it had been done, begged the same for herself and got it.

## modern-en · laelius · 27:26

When Laelius, in the presence of the Roman consuls, who, after sentencing Tiberius Gracchus, were prosecuting all who had had any familiarity with him, came to ask Caius Blosius, who had been Gracchus's chief friend, how much he would have done for him, and Blosius answered, "All things" — "What! all things?" said Laelius. "And what if he had ordered you to set fire to our temples?" — "He would never have ordered me that," Blosius replied. "But what if he had?" said Laelius. "I would have obeyed him," said the other. If he was as perfect a friend to Gracchus as the histories report, there was still no need to offend the consuls by so bold a confession; he might have kept his confidence in Gracchus's disposition to himself. But those who attack his answer as seditious miss the point, and do not see — as was the case — that Blosius had Gracchus's will in his pocket, both by the power of a friend and by his thorough knowledge of the man. They were more friends than citizens, more friends to each other than either enemies or friends to their country, more friends than they were friends to ambition or innovation. Having absolutely given themselves up to one another, each held the reins of the other's inclination absolutely; and if we suppose all this guided by virtue and conducted by reason — which it could not have been without — Blosius's answer was what it ought to be. If any of their actions had gone off the handle, they were not (by my measure of friendship) friends to one another, nor even to themselves. As for the rest, that answer sounds no worse than my own would, if someone asked me, "If your will should order you to kill your daughter, would you do it?" — and I answered yes. This expresses no agreement to such an act, since I have no suspicion of my own will, and as little of such a friend's. No eloquence in the world could dispossess me of my certainty about my friend's intentions and resolutions. There is not a single action of his, with whatever face it might wear, that I could not at first glance trace back to its true motive. Our souls were drawn so closely together, had regarded each other with such ardent affection and laid open the very bottom of our hearts to each other with the same affection, that I not only knew his as well as my own — in any concern of mine I would have trusted my interest more willingly with him than with myself.

Who asked Caius Blosius, in front of the Roman consuls prosecuting everyone who had been familiar with Tiberius Gracchus, how much he would have done for him — and got the answer: all things. Many at Rome thought and would usually say that the greatest of Scipio’s acts were in part due to him, his constant practice being to advance and support Scipio’s grandeur and renown without any care of his own; and with Fabricius he is one of the two ancients whose countenance and behaviour Montaigne says our people would think barbarous.

## modern-en · suidas · 30:24

As for the rest, they live in a country that is very pleasant and temperate, so that, as my witnesses tell me, it is rare to hear of anyone falling ill, and they assure me they have never seen any of the natives palsied, bleary-eyed, toothless, or bent with age. The country lies along the seashore, fenced on the inland side by great high mountains, with a stretch of about a hundred leagues between. They have plenty of fish and meat, none of which look like ours, and they eat them with no cookery beyond plain boiling, roasting, and grilling. The first man to ride in there on a horse, though in earlier voyages he had become acquainted and familiar with them, frightened them so badly with his centaur appearance that they killed him with their arrows before they could make out who he was. Their houses are very long, big enough to hold two or three hundred people, made of the bark of tall trees, one end stuck in the ground and the trees leaning on each other at the top to support one another, like some of our barns, where the roof comes right down to the ground and serves as side walls too. They have wood so hard that they cut with it and make their swords from it, and grills from it to grill their meat. Their beds are of cotton, slung from the roof like our sailors' hammocks, every man with his own — for the wives sleep apart from their husbands. They rise with the sun, and as soon as they are up, eat for the whole day, since they have no further meals. They do not drink at meals — as Suidas reports of certain other peoples of the East who never drank with their food — but drink very often during the rest of the day, and sometimes to a rousing pitch. Their drink is made of a certain root and is the colour of our claret, and they only ever drink it lukewarm. It keeps no more than two or three days; it has a slightly sharp, brisk taste, is not at all heady, but very kind to the stomach; laxative to strangers but a pleasant beverage to those used to it. Instead of bread they use a certain white compound, like coriander seeds; I have tasted it — the flavour is sweet and a little bland. The whole day is spent in dancing. The young men go off to hunt wild beasts with bows and arrows; meanwhile some of the women are busy heating their drink, which is their chief occupation. One of their old men, in the morning before they begin to eat, preaches to the whole household, walking from one end of the house to the other and repeating the same sentence over and over until he has completed the round — for their houses are at least a hundred yards long. Valour against their enemies and love toward their wives are the two heads of his sermon, never failing to remind them, in closing, that it is their wives who give them their drink warm and well-seasoned. The shape of their beds, ropes, swords, the wooden bracelets they tie around their wrists when they go to fight, and the great canes hollowed out at one end, by whose sound they keep the cadence of their dances, are to be seen in several places, and among them at my house. They shave themselves all over, and much more neatly than we do, with no razor but one of wood or stone. They believe in the immortality of the soul, and that those who have deserved well of the gods are lodged in that part of heaven where the sun rises, and the damned in the west.

The Greek lexicographer, cited for what he reports of some people of the East who drink only outside their meals.

## modern-en · achilles · 27:19

Nor will the very picture the Academy paints of it, as I read them, contradict me when I say this: the first frenzy that the son of Venus put into the heart of the lover at the sight of the bloom of a budding youth — to which they allowed all the brazen, passionate efforts that an immoderate ardour can produce — was founded simply on outward beauty, the false image of physical generation. It could not be founded on the soul, which was still hidden, only just beginning to emerge, and not yet ripe enough to bloom. If this frenzy seized a base spirit, the means by which it pressed its suit were rich presents, favours toward promotion, and such trumpery, all of which the Academy entirely rejects. If it seized a more generous soul, the courtship was correspondingly noble: philosophical instruction, exhortations to revere religion, to obey the laws, to die for one's country, examples of valour, prudence, and justice — the lover working to make himself acceptable through the grace and beauty of his soul, his body's beauty being long past — hoping, by this companionship of minds, to set up a firmer and more lasting contract. When such a courtship reached its goal in due season (for what they did not require in the lover, namely patience and discretion in pursuit, they strictly required in the beloved, since he had to judge of an inward beauty hard to know and hidden), then there arose in the beloved the desire for a spiritual conception by means of a spiritual beauty. This was the main thing; the bodily was incidental and secondary — the reverse of the lover's case. For this reason they preferred the beloved, maintaining that the gods preferred him too, and they greatly blame the poet Aeschylus for having, in the loves of Achilles and Patroclus, given the lover's part to Achilles, who was in the first beardless flower of his youth and the handsomest of the Greeks. After this general union, with the sovereign and worthiest part presiding, governing, and doing its proper offices, great advantages followed, they say, for both private and public life — it made up the strength and power of the countries where it prevailed, and the chief security of liberty and justice. The healthy loves of Harmodius and Aristogiton are their examples. Hence they called it sacred and divine, and held that nothing was hostile to it except the violence of tyrants and the baseness of the common people. Finally, all that can be said in favour of the Academy is that this was a love which ended in friendship — which fits well enough with the Stoic definition of love:

## modern-en · patroclus · 27:19

Nor will the very picture the Academy paints of it, as I read them, contradict me when I say this: the first frenzy that the son of Venus put into the heart of the lover at the sight of the bloom of a budding youth — to which they allowed all the brazen, passionate efforts that an immoderate ardour can produce — was founded simply on outward beauty, the false image of physical generation. It could not be founded on the soul, which was still hidden, only just beginning to emerge, and not yet ripe enough to bloom. If this frenzy seized a base spirit, the means by which it pressed its suit were rich presents, favours toward promotion, and such trumpery, all of which the Academy entirely rejects. If it seized a more generous soul, the courtship was correspondingly noble: philosophical instruction, exhortations to revere religion, to obey the laws, to die for one's country, examples of valour, prudence, and justice — the lover working to make himself acceptable through the grace and beauty of his soul, his body's beauty being long past — hoping, by this companionship of minds, to set up a firmer and more lasting contract. When such a courtship reached its goal in due season (for what they did not require in the lover, namely patience and discretion in pursuit, they strictly required in the beloved, since he had to judge of an inward beauty hard to know and hidden), then there arose in the beloved the desire for a spiritual conception by means of a spiritual beauty. This was the main thing; the bodily was incidental and secondary — the reverse of the lover's case. For this reason they preferred the beloved, maintaining that the gods preferred him too, and they greatly blame the poet Aeschylus for having, in the loves of Achilles and Patroclus, given the lover's part to Achilles, who was in the first beardless flower of his youth and the handsomest of the Greeks. After this general union, with the sovereign and worthiest part presiding, governing, and doing its proper offices, great advantages followed, they say, for both private and public life — it made up the strength and power of the countries where it prevailed, and the chief security of liberty and justice. The healthy loves of Harmodius and Aristogiton are their examples. Hence they called it sacred and divine, and held that nothing was hostile to it except the violence of tyrants and the baseness of the common people. Finally, all that can be said in favour of the Academy is that this was a love which ended in friendship — which fits well enough with the Stoic definition of love:

## modern-en · eudamidas · 27:28

If, in the friendship I am speaking of, one could give to the other, the receiver of the favour would be the one putting his friend in his debt. Each of them, contending above all to be useful to the other, the one who provides the opportunity is the generous one — giving his friend the satisfaction of doing for him the thing he most desires to do. When the philosopher Diogenes was short of money, he used to say that he was reclaiming it from his friends, not asking for it. To show how this works in practice, let me give you an ancient and singular example. Eudamidas, a Corinthian, had two friends: Charixenus the Sicyonian and Areteus the Corinthian. Coming to die poor, while his two friends were rich, he made his will in this fashion: "I bequeath to Areteus the keeping of my mother, to provide for her in her old age; and to Charixenus I bequeath the task of marrying my daughter, and giving her as good a dowry as he is able; and should one of these die first, I substitute the survivor in his place." The first to see the will laughed at it, but the legatees, when they heard, accepted it with very great content. One of them, Charixenus, died five days later; the whole charge now falling on Areteus, he took care of the old woman with great affection, and out of the five talents he had to his name he gave two and a half as dowry for his own only daughter, and two and a half as dowry for Eudamidas's daughter, and held both weddings on the same day.

A Corinthian who died poor with two rich friends, and left his mother’s maintenance to Areteus and his daughter’s marriage to Charixenus — a will everyone laughed at and the legatees accepted with content. Montaigne says the force of friendship shows more in leaving them the chance of the benefit than in their discharging it.

Callicles in Plato says that the furthest reaches of philosophy are harmful, and advises against diving into it beyond the point where it pays off. Taken moderately, he says, it is pleasant and useful, but pushed too far it leaves a man brutish and vicious, scornful of religion and the common laws, an enemy to civil society and to all human pleasures, useless for any public office, unable to help others or even himself, and a ready target for every kind of insult and injury. ## modern-en · zenobia · 29:11

Marriage is a solemn, religious tie, and so the pleasure we draw from it should be a sober and serious delight, mixed with a certain gravity — a discreet, conscientious sort of pleasure. And since its chief end is generation, some have questioned whether, when men are out of hope of children — too old, or when the wife is already pregnant — it is lawful to embrace our wives. It is homicide, according to Plato. Certain nations — the Mohammedan among others — abhor any union with women who are pregnant; others, with women who are in their courses. Zenobia would let her husband in only for a single encounter, after which she sent him off to manage his own appetites for the whole period of her conception, and only after that would receive him again — a brave and generous example of conjugal continence. It was, no doubt, from some lascivious poet, himself in great straits for a little of this sport, that Plato borrowed the story that Jupiter was once so hot for his wife that, not having the patience to wait for the couch, he threw her down on the floor, where the violence of pleasure made him forget the great and important decisions he had just taken with the other gods in their heavenly council, and made him boast that he had had as good a time of it as when, unknown to her parents, he first took her maidenhead.

Who would admit her husband for one encounter only and then left him to himself for the whole time of her conception — a brave and generous example, Montaigne says, of conjugal continence.

## modern-en · aelius-verus · 29:12

The kings of Persia used to invite their wives to the start of their feasts; but once the wine had really begun to work, and they meant to give pleasure its head, they sent them back to their private quarters, so that they would not have to take part in their immoderate lust, sending in other women in their stead, with whom they were not bound by the same decorum. Not all pleasures and all forms of gratification fit all persons. Epaminondas had put a young man in prison for certain debaucheries; when Pelopidas pleaded that, at his request, the young man might be released, Epaminondas refused; but he granted it at once, at the first word, to a wench of his who made the same plea — saying that this was a favour fit for one such as she, but not for a general. Sophocles, joint praetor with Pericles, happened to see a fine boy go by and exclaimed, "What a charming boy!" "That might do very well," answered Pericles, "for someone other than a praetor, who must keep not only his hands but his eyes chaste." The emperor Aelius Verus answered his wife, who reproached him with his love of other women, that he did it on a conscientious account, since marriage was a name of honour and dignity, not of wanton and lascivious desire; and our church history preserves with great reverence the memory of a woman who left her husband because she would not yield to his indecent and inordinate desires. In short, there is no pleasure so just and lawful that intemperance and excess in it should not be condemned.

The emperor who answered his wife’s reproaches about other women by saying that marriage was a name of honour and dignity, not of wanton desire. The modern edition spells him Aelius.

## modern-en · gallio · 29:16

Human wisdom misuses its talent as much when it sets to work cutting down the number and sweetness of the pleasures that are naturally our due, as it uses it well when it artfully dresses up and disguises the ills of life to soften the feel of them. Had I been in charge, I would have taken another, more natural course — one which, to tell the truth, is both convenient and holy, and which perhaps I could have set within bounds. But our spiritual and bodily physicians, as if by mutual agreement, can find no other way to cure the body's and the soul's infirmities than by misery and pain. To this end, vigils, fasts, hair-shirts, distant and solitary banishments, perpetual imprisonments, scourges, and other afflictions have been introduced — but on the understanding that they will sting, that they will be real afflictions; not turn out as they did with one Gallio, who, having been exiled to Lesbos, was soon reported back in Rome to be living merry as the day is long, and that what had been laid on him as a penance had turned to his pleasure. The Senate then thought fit to recall him home to his wife and family, and confine him to his own house, in order to suit the punishment to his actual feelings. To the man whom fasting makes more healthful and more lively, and to the man whose palate prefers fish to flesh, the prescription of these would have no curative effect — any more than drugs swallowed with appetite and pleasure cure the patient. The bitterness of the potion and the patient's aversion are necessary for the cure to work. The nature that would eat rhubarb like buttered turnips would frustrate the use and virtue of it; it must be something to trouble and disturb the stomach, that must purge and cure it. And here the common rule — that contraries cure — fails, for in this one case ill is cured by ill.

Exiled to Lesbos and found to be living there as merry as the day was long, so that the Senate recalled him and confined him to his own house with his wife and family — to fit the punishment to his feeling.

## modern-en · flaminius · 30:0

When King Pyrrhus invaded Italy, after surveying the order of the army the Romans had sent out to meet him, he said: "I do not know what kind of barbarians these may be" — for so the Greeks called all other nations — "but the disposition of this army that I see before me has nothing barbarous in it." The Greeks said as much of the army Flaminius brought into their country; and Philip, watching from a height the order and lay-out of the Roman camp Publius Sulpicius Galba had pitched in his kingdom, made a similar remark. ## modern-en · arsac · 30:10

It seems that in this great body of the earth there are two sorts of motion, as in our own — one natural and the other feverish. When I think of the impression our river, the Dordogne, has made in my time on its right bank, how in twenty years it has gained so much ground and undermined the foundations of so many houses, I take it for an unusual agitation; for if it had always run that way, or were to do so in future, the look of the world would be wholly changed. But rivers alter their course, beating now against one bank, now the other, and sometimes keeping quietly to their channel. I am not speaking of sudden floods, the causes of which everyone understands. In Médoc, by the seashore, my brother, Sieur d'Arsac, sees an estate he owned there buried under the sands that the sea throws up before it; the tops of some houses are still to be seen, and his rents and lands have been turned into pitiful, barren scrub. The people of the place say that of late years the sea has been driving so hard against them that they have lost more than four leagues of land. These sands are her outriders, and we can now see great mounds of moving sand marching half a league ahead of her, taking the land as they go.

Montaigne’s brother, who watches an estate of his in Medoc being buried under the sand the sea drives before it, the tops of some houses still showing and his rents turned to barren pasture.

## modern-en · leonidas · 30:37

— he who gives up nothing of his self-possession in the face of imminent death, who dying still throws his enemy a fierce and disdainful look, is overcome not by us but by fortune; he is killed, not conquered. The most valiant are sometimes the most unfortunate. There are defeats more triumphant than victories. Those four sister victories — the fairest the sun ever looked on, of Salamis, Plataea, Mycale, and Sicily — never dared to set their united glory against the single glory of the rout of King Leonidas and his men at the pass of Thermopylae. Who ever ran with a more glorious purpose, a higher ambition, toward winning a battle than Captain Iscolas did toward the certain loss of one? Who could have come up with a more subtle device to secure his own safety than he found to assure his own destruction? He was sent to defend a certain pass of the Peloponnese against the Arcadians; finding it utterly impossible, given the lie of the ground and the imbalance of forces, and seeing that all who faced the enemy must inevitably be left dead on the spot, yet judging it unworthy of his own virtue and magnanimity, and of the Lacedaemonian name, to fail in any part of his duty, he chose a middle course between those two extremes. He saved the youngest and fittest of his men for the service and defence of their country and sent them back; with the rest, whose loss would be of less moment, he resolved to hold the pass and, by their deaths, make the enemy pay as dearly as possible for getting through. And so it fell out: surrounded on all sides by the Arcadians, he and his men, after killing a great many of the enemy, were cut to pieces. Is there a single trophy dedicated to the conquerors that was not far more due to those who lost? The part of true conquering lies in the encounter, not in the coming out the other side; the honour of valour consists in fighting, not in subduing.

Whose discomfiture at the pass of Thermopylae, Montaigne says, outweighs the four sister victories of Salamis, Plataea, Mycale and Sicily put together.

He saved the youngest and fittest of his men for the service and defence of their country and sent them back; with the rest, whose loss would be of less moment, he resolved to hold the pass and, by their deaths, make the enemy pay as dearly as possible for getting through. And so it fell out: surrounded on all sides by the Arcadians, he and his men, after killing a great many of the enemy, were cut to pieces. Is there a single trophy dedicated to the conquerors that was not far more due to those who lost? The part of true conquering lies in the encounter, not in the coming out the other side; the honour of valour consists in fighting, not in subduing.

Set to hold a pass of Peloponnesus against the Arcadians with no possibility of doing it, he sent the youngest and most active of his men home for their country’s service and held the pass with the rest until every one of them was cut to pieces. Montaigne asks whether the trophy was not more due to the conquered.

The men there have several wives, and the more wives the higher their reputation for valour. And it is one very remarkable feature of their marriages that the same jealousy our wives use to keep us from the friendship and intimacy of other women, theirs use to further their husbands' desires and to procure them many partners. Above all things concerned for their husbands' honour, they make it their chief care to seek out and bring in as many companions as they can, since this is held to be evidence of their husband's worth. Most of our ladies will cry out that this is monstrous; in truth, it is not so, but a truly matrimonial virtue of the highest order. In the Bible, Sarah, with Leah and Rachel, the two wives of Jacob, gave the most beautiful of their handmaids to their husbands; Livia, in her own interest, indulged Augustus's passions for other women; and the wife of King Deiotarus, Stratonice, not only gave up a beautiful young maid in her service to her husband's embraces, but carefully brought up the children he had by her and helped them on to the succession of their father's crown.

Who with Leah and Rachel gave the most beautiful of her handmaids to her husband — Montaigne’s scriptural parallel to the cannibal wives who seek out companions for their husbands.

Three of these people, not foreseeing how dear a knowledge of the corruptions of this part of the world would one day cost their happiness and peace of mind — nor that their dealings with us are leading, as I take them to be, straight to their ruin (poor wretches, to let themselves be taken in by the desire for novelty, leaving the serenity of their own sky to come so far to gape at ours!) — were at Rouen when the late King Charles IX was there. The king himself talked with them a good while; they were shown our fashions, our pomp, the shape of a great city. Afterwards someone asked their opinion, wanting to know what among all the things they had seen they thought most worth admiring. To which they answered three things — of which I have forgotten the third, and am sorry for it, but two I still remember. They said, first, that they thought it very strange that so many tall men, bearded, strong, well-armed, who stood about the king (probably they meant the Swiss Guard), should submit to obeying a child, and not rather pick out one of their own number to command. Secondly (they have a way of speaking in their language by which they call men the halves of one another) they had noticed that there were among us men full and crammed with every sort of good, while their other halves were begging at their doors, lean and half-starved with hunger and poverty; and they thought it strange that these needy halves were able to bear such inequality and injustice, and did not take the others by the throat or set fire to their houses.

At Rouen when three of the cannibals were brought there, and who talked with them a good while. They said it was strange that so many tall bearded armed men should submit to obey a child.

## modern-en · don-john-of-austria · 31:4

Among one Indian nation there is a praiseworthy custom: when anything goes against them in some encounter or battle, they publicly ask pardon of the sun, who is their god, as though they had done some unjust act, always crediting their good or bad fortune to divine justice and submitting their own judgment and reason to it. It is enough for a Christian to believe that all things come from God, to receive them with acknowledgment of his divine and unsearchable wisdom, and so to accept them gratefully with whatever face they may wear. But I do not approve of the common practice of trying to confirm and support our religion by the success of our enterprises. Our belief has foundation enough without needing to be authorised by events. The people, accustomed to such plausible arguments, well-suited to their taste, are likely, when those arguments fail, to stagger in their faith too. So in this war we are now engaged in on account of religion, those who had the upper hand at the affair of Rochelabeille made loud boasts of it as an infallible approval of their cause, and then, when they had to excuse their misfortunes at Moncontour and Jarnac by calling them fatherly scourges and corrections — "because the people were not yet wholly at their mercy" — they show plainly enough what it is to draw two sorts of grist out of the same sack, and to blow hot and cold with the same mouth. It would be better to ground the common people in the solid, real foundations of truth. There was a fine naval battle won a few months ago under the command of Don John of Austria against the Turks; but it has also pleased God at other times to let us see victories just as great at our own expense. In short, it is a hard thing to reduce divine matters to our scales without losing a great deal of the weight in the spillage. And anyone who would try to give a reason why Arius and his Pope Leo, the principal heads of the Arian heresy, both died, at different times, of such similar and strange deaths (for, called away from disputation by a griping in the bowels, they both suddenly gave up the ghost on the privy), and would aggravate this divine vengeance by the circumstances of the place, might as well throw in the death of Heliogabalus, who was also killed in a privy. And Irenaeus, indeed, came to a similar end. God, pleased to show us that the good have something else to hope for, and the wicked something else to fear, than the fortunes or misfortunes of this world, manages and applies them according to his own hidden will and pleasure, and deprives us of the means of foolishly making a profit of them. So those people delude themselves who try to dive into these mysteries by the strength of human reason. They never strike one blow without taking two in return — of which St. Augustine makes a great proof against his opponents. It is a contest decided more by strength of memory than by force of reason. We must content ourselves with the light the sun is pleased to communicate to us by his rays; and whoever lifts up his eyes to take in more, let him not think it strange if, for the reward of his presumption, he loses his sight.

Under whose command the fine naval battle against the Turks was won a few months before Montaigne wrote — a victory he will not let anyone use as proof of a cause, since God has let us see as great ones at our own expense.

## modern-en · lucilius · 32:2

But to push contempt of death so far as to use it for clearing our minds of honours, riches, dignities, and the other gifts we call goods of fortune — as if reason alone were not enough to persuade us to give them up without this added injunction — I had never seen it commanded or practised until I came across this passage of Seneca. He was advising Lucilius, a man of great power and authority close to the emperor, to give up his lavish and pleasure-seeking way of life and retire to some quiet, solitary, philosophical existence. When Lucilius raised difficulties, Seneca said: "My opinion is that either you leave that life of yours, or life itself. I would advise the gentler way: untie, rather than break, the knot you have rashly tied. But if it cannot be untied otherwise, then break it cleanly. No man is so cowardly that he would not rather fall once than be always falling." I would have expected such counsel from Stoic severity, but it is stranger coming, as it does, from Epicurus, who writes the same thing on a similar occasion to Idomeneus. And I think I have noticed something like it — though with Christian moderation — among our own people.

The man of power about the emperor whom Seneca advises either to leave that life of his or life itself: better once to fall than to be always falling.

## modern-en · abra · 32:3

St. Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, that famous enemy of the Arian heresy, was in Syria when word reached him that Abra, his only daughter, whom he had left at home under her mother's care, was being sought in marriage by the greatest noblemen of the country — a virtuous, well-brought-up girl, beautiful, rich, and in the flower of her youth. He wrote back to her (as the record shows) that she should remove her affection from all the pleasures and advantages being offered, since on his travels he had found a far greater and worthier match for her: a husband of much greater power and magnificence, who would clothe her in robes and jewels of inestimable value. His aim was to wean her from the appetite for worldly delights and to join her wholly to God. And since the nearest and surest route to that, as he saw it, was his daughter's death, he never stopped praying and pleading with the Almighty to please call her out of this world and take her to himself. And it came to pass: soon after his return she died, at which he showed a singular joy. This seems to outdo the others, since he turns to this method from the start where they only resort to it secondarily, and it was on his own only daughter. But I will not leave out the rest of the story, even though it suits my purpose. St. Hilary's wife, learning from him how their daughter's death had been brought about by his deliberate prayer, and how much happier she was to be removed from this world than to have remained in it, conceived so vivid a sense of eternal and heavenly bliss that she begged her husband with utmost insistence to do the same for her. And God, at their joint request, soon called her too — a death embraced with singular and mutual contentment.

St Hilary’s only daughter, left at home under her mother’s eye, sought in marriage by the greatest noblemen of the country, and prayed out of the world by her father.

may reasonably make us expect her to show all sorts of faces. Can there be a clearer act of justice than this? ## modern-en · constantine-founder · 33:7

Doesn't she seem to play the artist here? Constantine, son of Helena, founded the empire of Constantinople, and many ages later, Constantine, son of Helen, brought it to its end. Sometimes she likes to mimic our miracles. We are told that when King Clovis was besieging Angoulême, the walls fell down on their own by divine favour; and Bouchet has it from some author that when King Robert was laying siege to a city and had slipped away from the siege to keep the feast of St. Aignan at Orleans, the walls of the besieged city collapsed in sudden ruin, without any assault, while he was at his devotions in a certain part of the Mass. But she did just the opposite in our Milan wars: Captain Rense was besieging Arona for us and had dug a mine under a great stretch of the wall; when the mine was sprung, the wall lifted off its foundations — and then dropped back down, whole and entire, exactly on its base, so that the besieged took no harm at all from the attempt.

Who founded the empire of Constantinople.

## modern-en · jason-of-pheres · 33:8

Sometimes she plays the physician. Jason of Pheres, given up by the doctors because of an abscess in his chest, decided to rid himself of his pain at least by death, and threw himself recklessly into the thick of the enemy in a battle. He was so luckily wounded clean through the body that the abscess burst and he was completely cured. Did she not also outdo the painter Protogenes at his own art? He had finished a picture of a dog, panting and out of breath, well rendered in every other part but he could not get the foam and slaver coming from its mouth quite right. Furious with his work, he snatched up his sponge, which had soaked up various colours from cleaning his brushes, and hurled it at the picture meaning to ruin it. Fortune guided the sponge to land just at the dog's mouth, where it produced what all his skill could not. Does she not sometimes direct our plans and correct them? Isabel, Queen of England, sailing from Zealand back into her own kingdom with an army to support her son against her husband, would have been lost had she landed at the port she meant to, where the enemy lay in wait; but fortune, against her wishes, drove her into another harbour where she landed safely. And that man of old who, throwing a stone at a dog, hit and killed his mother-in-law — was he not right to declare:

Given over by the physicians for an imposthume in his breast, he threw himself into the thickest of the enemy to be rid of the pain by death at least — and was so fortunately wounded through the body that the imposthume broke and he was cured.

## modern-en · icetes · 33:10

Icetes had hired two soldiers to kill Timoleon at Adrana in Sicily. They picked their moment while he was at a sacrifice and pushed into the crowd. As they were signalling to each other that the time had come, a third man stepped in and felled one of them with a sword stroke across the head, leaving him dead on the spot, and ran off. The other, thinking himself discovered and as good as dead, fled to the altar and begged for mercy, promising to confess the whole plot. As he was doing so, laying out the full conspiracy, the third man — the one who had run — was caught and dragged through the crowd as a murderer, hauled before Timoleon and the chief men of the assembly. There he cried for pardon, pleading that he had justly killed his father's murderer. He proved it on the spot through reliable witnesses whom good fortune had conveniently provided — that his father had indeed been killed in the city of Leontini by the very man on whom he had now taken revenge. He was at once awarded ten Attic minae for having had the good fortune, by setting out to avenge his father's death, to preserve the life of the common father of Sicily. Fortune, truly, in her workings exceeds all the rules of human prudence.

Who contracted with two soldiers to kill Timoleon at Adrana in Sicily.

## modern-en · ignatius-father · 33:11

To finish: is there not a clear show of her favour, generosity, and even piety in this episode? Ignatius the father and Ignatius the son, proscribed by the Roman triumvirs, agreed on the generous act of dying by each other's hands and so cheating the cruelty of the tyrants. Swords drawn, they rushed full tilt at one another, and fortune so guided the points that they each inflicted an equally mortal wound — while granting their brave friendship just enough strength left to draw out the bloody swords and embrace one another in their dying. They held each other so closely and so warmly that the executioner cut off both their heads at once, leaving the bodies still locked together in that noble bond, their wounds joined mouth to mouth, lovingly sucking in each other's last blood and life.

Who with his son, proscribed by the triumvirs, ran on his son’s sword as the son ran on his, so that the two mortal wounds were equal and the executioner cut off both heads at once, the bodies still locked together.

## modern-en · giraldus · 34:1

I have heard — to the great shame of the age we live in — that two of the most learned men of our day died so poor they had hardly bread to put in their mouths: Lilius Gregorius Giraldus in Italy and Sebastianus Castalio in Germany. I am sure there are a thousand men who would have invited them into their families on advantageous terms, or relieved them where they were, had they only known of their want. The world is not so universally corrupted; I know a man who would gladly use the estate his ancestors left him, for as long as fortune allows him to enjoy it, to shelter rare and remarkable people of any kind whom misfortune sometimes persecutes to the last extreme, from the dangers of want — at least to place them in such a condition that they would have to be hard to please not to be content.

Who died in Italy so poor he had scarce bread to put in his mouth — one of the two most excellent men for learning whose want Montaigne says the age should be ashamed of.

## modern-en · massinissa · 35:3

so were we; but, like people who put out the day's light by burning artificial light, we have, with borrowed forms and fashions, destroyed our own. And it is plain that custom alone makes impossible what is otherwise not so at all. For of those peoples who know nothing of clothing, some live in the same temperatures we do, and some in much colder climates. Besides, our most tender parts are always exposed to the air — the eyes, mouth, nose, ears — and our country labourers, like our ancestors in earlier times, go with their chests and bellies open. Had we been born with a built-in need for skirts and breeches, no doubt nature would have armoured the parts she meant to expose to the seasons with a thicker skin, as she has done at the fingertips and the soles of the feet. And why should this seem hard to believe? I notice much more distance between my own dress and that of one of our country labourers than between his and that of a man who has no other covering but his skin. How many men, especially in Turkey, go naked out of devotion? Someone asked a beggar, whom he saw walking around in his shirt in the depth of winter, as cheerful as a man wrapped up to the ears in furs, how he could stand to go like that. "Why, sir," he answered, "you go with your face bare; I am all face." The Italians tell a story of the Duke of Florence's fool. When the duke, warmly wrapped, asked him how he, so thinly clad, could bear the cold the duke himself could barely endure, the fool answered: "Try my recipe — put on all the clothes you own at once, and you'll feel no more cold than I do." King Massinissa, into extreme old age, could never be persuaded to cover his head, no matter how cold, stormy, or rainy the weather; the same is told of the Emperor Severus. Herodotus tells us that in the battles between Egyptians and Persians, both he and others observed that of the bodies left on the field the skulls of the Egyptians were beyond comparison harder than those of the Persians, because the latter had gone with their heads always covered from infancy — first with caps, then with turbans — while the others kept theirs always shaved and bare. King Agesilaus, into a decrepit old age, wore the same clothes in winter that he wore in summer. Caesar, says Suetonius, always marched at the head of his army, usually on foot, bareheaded whether it rained or shone; as much is said of Hannibal:

Who to an extreme old age could never be prevailed on to cover his head, in whatever weather.

## modern-en · varro · 35:6

A Venetian who has lived for a long time in Pegu, and who has lately come back from there, writes that the men and women of that kingdom, though they cover all their other parts, always go barefoot and even ride that way. And Plato strongly advises, for the health of the whole body, to give the head and feet no clothing other than what nature has provided. The man whom the Poles have elected as their king since ours came back from there — one of the greatest princes of the age — never wears gloves, and whatever the weather, in winter or otherwise, wears no other cap outdoors than he wears at home. I, on the other hand, can't stand to be unbuttoned or untied; my neighbouring labourers would feel themselves in chains if they were laced up like me. Varro thinks that when it was decreed we should be bareheaded in the presence of the gods and the magistrate, it was set up more for the sake of health, to harden us against the weather, than out of any sense of reverence. And since we are now on the subject of cold, and since the French used to wear all sorts of colours — not I, since I rarely wear anything but black or white, in imitation of my father — let us add another story from Captain Martin du Bellay, who reports that on the march to Luxembourg he saw such a great frost that the troops' ration-wine was cut with hatchets and wedges and given out to the soldiers by weight, who carried it away in baskets. And Ovid:

Who thinks the rule that we go bare before the gods and the magistrate was made for health and to inure us to the weather rather than out of reverence.

At the mouth of Lake Maeotis the frosts are so sharp that on the very same ground where Mithridates' lieutenant had fought the enemy dry-shod and given them a serious defeat, the following summer he won a naval victory over them on the same place. Whose lieutenant beat the enemy dry-foot at the mouth of Lake Maeotis in a frost so sharp, and beat them again in a naval battle on the same water the summer after.

## modern-en · pausanias-plataea · 36:10

In the great battle of Plataea, which the Greeks under Pausanias won against Mardonius and the Persians, the victors, when dividing the glory of the action according to their custom, gave the Spartan nation the highest credit for valour in the engagement. The Spartans, expert judges of virtue, came to decide which particular Spartan deserved the honour of having behaved best on that occasion. They found that Aristodemus had risked himself with greater bravery than any other; but they would not award him the prize, on the grounds that his courage had been driven by a wish to clear his name of the disgrace he had earned at Thermopylae and to die well so as to wipe out that earlier stain.

The Spartan who commanded at Plataea. Montaigne has already told how his own mother threw the first stone towards his death.

## modern-en · aristodemus · 36:10

In the great battle of Plataea, which the Greeks under Pausanias won against Mardonius and the Persians, the victors, when dividing the glory of the action according to their custom, gave the Spartan nation the highest credit for valour in the engagement. The Spartans, expert judges of virtue, came to decide which particular Spartan deserved the honour of having behaved best on that occasion. When Stilpo had escaped the burning of his town, where he lost his wife, his children, and his goods, Demetrius Poliorcetes, seeing him appear undisturbed amid such a ruin of his country, asked him whether he had suffered no loss. Stilpo answered, No; and that, thank God, nothing of his had been lost. This was also what the philosopher Antisthenes meant when he said wryly that "a man should furnish himself with such things as would float, and that could escape the storm with their owner." And indeed a wise man never loses anything if he has himself. When the city of Nola was destroyed by the barbarians, Paulinus, who was bishop of the place, having lost everything he had and being himself a prisoner, prayed like this: "O Lord, keep me from feeling this loss; for you know that they have not yet touched anything of what is truly mine." The riches that made him rich and the goods that made him good were still intact. This is what it is to choose treasures that can defend themselves from plunder and violence, and to hide them in a place no one can enter and that can only be betrayed by ourselves. Wives, children, goods are to be had, and especially health, by those who can get them; but we are not to set our hearts on them so far that our happiness depends on them. We must reserve a back-shop, wholly our own and entirely free, in which to set up our true liberty, our chief solitude and retreat. There we are mostly to keep our own company, and so privately that no foreign acquaintance or commerce is admitted; there to laugh and to talk as if without wife, children, goods, retinue, or attendance — so that when it falls out that we must lose any or all of them, it will be no new thing for us to be without them. We have a mind pliable enough in itself to be company; it has what is needed to attack and defend, to receive and to give. Let us not, then, fear that we shall languish in this solitude under a dreary emptiness.

Who escaped the burning of his town having lost wife, children and goods, and told Demetrius Poliorcetes that he had received no loss, since fortune had nothing of his — and who, oppressed with age, is said to have purposely hastened his end by drinking pure wine.

the contagion is very dangerous in a crowd. ## modern-en · annibale-caro · 39:15

On the subject of letters, I will add this to what has been said: it is a kind of writing in which my friends think I can do something; and I am willing to confess that I would have preferred to publish my whimsies in that form than in any other, had I had someone to write to. But I lacked the kind of settled correspondence I once had — one that would draw me to it, raise my fancy, and sustain me. As for trafficking with the wind, as some others have done, and forging imaginary names to address letters to, on a serious subject — I could only ever do this in a dream, being a sworn enemy of every kind of falsification. I should have been more diligent and more confident if I had had a judicious and indulgent friend to address, rather than exposing myself like this to the various judgments of a whole public; and I am much mistaken if I would not have done better that way. I have naturally a humorous and familiar style; but it is a style of my own, not fit for public business — like the language I speak, too compact, irregular, abrupt, idiosyncratic. As for letters of ceremony that have no substance beyond a polite weaving of courteous words, I am hopelessly at a loss; I have neither faculty nor taste for those tedious offerings of service and affection; I believe little of them from others, and I would not forgive myself for saying to others more than I myself believe. This is, no doubt, very far from current practice; for there has never been so abject and servile a prostitution of offers: life, soul, devotion, adoration, vassal, slave, and I can't tell what else — all such expressions so commonly and indifferently bandied about by everyone to everyone, that when they want to declare a greater and more respectful inclination on more deserving occasions, they have nothing left to express it with. I have a deep loathing of any whiff of flattery, which is why I naturally drop into a shy, rough, blunt way of speaking which, to those who do not know me, may seem to smack a little of disdain. I honour most those to whom I show the least honour, and where my soul moves with the greatest cheerfulness I easily forget the ceremonies of look and gesture, and offer myself faintly and bluntly to those to whom I am most devoted — they should, I think, read it in my heart; and the wording of what I say only injures the love I have inwardly conceived. As for welcoming, taking leave, giving thanks, accosting, offering one's services, and all those verbal formalities that the ceremonious laws of our modern civility prescribe, I know no one as stupidly unfurnished with such language as myself; and I have never been employed in writing letters of favour or recommendation without the man for whom they were written thinking my intervention cold and inadequate. The Italians are great printers of letters; I believe I have at least a hundred separate volumes of them, of which Annibale Caro's seem to me the best. If all the paper I have scribbled to the ladies, back when my hand was really prompted by passion, were still in existence, perhaps one might find a page worthy to be passed on to our young men in love, who are bewildered by that fury. I always write my letters at top speed — so headlong that, though I write quite illegibly, I would rather do it myself than employ another, since I can find no one able to keep up with me; and I never copy any out again. I have got the great ones who know me used to enduring my blots and crossings out, and to paper without fold or margin. The letters that cost me the most pains are the worst; when I begin dragging it along by the ears, it's a sign that I am not really in it. I throw myself in without forethought or design; the first word starts the second, and so on to the end of the chapter. The letters of this age consist more in fine edges and prefaces than in matter. Just as I would rather write two letters than fold and seal one (and always give that job to someone else), so, when the real business of my letter is finished, I would gladly hand it on to another to add those long harangues, offers, and prayers we put at the bottom — and I would be glad if some new custom would relieve us of that trouble; likewise of heading them with a long string of qualities and titles, which, for fear of mistakes, I have often left out altogether, especially to men of the long robe and of finance. There are so many new offices, such a shuffling and arranging of titles of honour, that it is hard to get them right; and yet, since they are so dearly bought, they cannot be altered or omitted without giving offence. I find it equally in bad taste to clutter the fronts and inscriptions of the books we send to the press with the like.

Whose printed letters Montaigne thinks the best of the hundred volumes of them he owns.

## modern-en · scipio-aemilianus · 39:0

One more word by way of comparison between these two. There are to be gathered, out of the writings of Cicero and the younger Pliny (who, in my opinion, resembled his uncle in his temperament very little), endless evidences of an immeasurably ambitious nature; and among others, this one: that both of them publicly solicit the historians of their time not to leave them out of their memoirs. And fortune, as if in spite, has kept the vanity of those requests on record down to our own day, while she long ago consigned the histories themselves to oblivion. But this surpasses any meanness of spirit in men of their standing — to think to draw great renown from chatter and verbal display, even publishing their private letters to their friends, and so doing it that, though some of them were never sent (the chance having gone), they still brought them to light with this fine excuse: that they were unwilling to waste their labours and lucubrations. Was it really becoming for two consuls of Rome, sovereign magistrates of the republic that ruled the world, to spend their leisure crafting clever, elegant letters in order to get a reputation for being good at their own mother tongue? Even a wretched schoolmaster, whose trade was teaching for a living, could hardly have done worse. If the deeds of Xenophon and Caesar had not far surpassed their eloquence, I scarcely believe they would have taken the pains to record them; they made it their business to recommend not their speaking but their doing. And if the perfection of eloquence could have added a lustre worthy of a great man, certainly Scipio and Laelius would never have surrendered the honour of their comedies, with all the luxuriance and elegance of the Latin tongue, to an African slave; for the work was theirs — its beauty and excellence say so clearly enough; Terence himself confesses as much; and I would take it ill from anyone who tried to dispossess me of that belief.

The Scipio who with Laelius is said to have resigned the honour of his comedies to an African — and who would never have done it, Montaigne says, if eloquence had added a lustre suitable to a great person. Not the Africanus who crossed to Syphax, nor Pompey’s father-in-law, nor the high priest. After two triumphs and two consulships he went an embassy with no more than seven servants in his train.

It is a kind of mockery and offence to praise a man for qualities unsuited to his station, even when they are otherwise commendable in themselves — qualities that should not, in any case, be his chief talent. They settle their household affairs, commend themselves to friends, sing, preach, address the crowd, even break out into jokes and drink to their companions, quite as composedly as Socrates did.

Who answered Lysimachus’s threat to kill him: thou wilt do a brave feat, to attain the force of a cantharides. His saying, set beside Hegesias’s, is that it is not reasonable a wise man should hazard himself for his country and endanger wisdom for a company of fools.

## modern-en · john-of-portugal · 40:8

When the kings of Castile banished the Jews from their lands, John, King of Portugal, in return for eight crowns a head, sold them refuge in his own kingdom for a limited period, on condition that when the period expired they were to leave, and he would furnish ships to transport them to Africa. The day came, and they were given to understand that any who remained in the kingdom afterwards would become slaves; the vessels provided were poorly equipped; and those who embarked were treated brutally and shamefully by the crews, who, among other indignities, kept them crisscrossing at sea — now forward, now back — until they had used up all their provisions and were forced to buy more from the sailors at extortionate prices for so long that they were not set on shore until they had been stripped to their very shirts. When news of this inhuman treatment reached those who had remained behind, the greater part of them resolved to accept slavery; some made a show of converting. Emmanuel, John's successor, on coming to the throne first set them at liberty, then changed his mind and ordered them out of the country, assigning three ports for their departure. He hoped, says Bishop Osorius — no contemptible Latin historian of these recent times — that since the favour of liberty he had granted them had failed to convert them to Christianity, the difficulty of trusting themselves to the mercy of the sailors and of abandoning a country in which they were now settled and had grown rich, in order to expose themselves in strange and unknown regions, would at last do it. But, finding himself mistaken in this expectation, and that they were all resolved on the voyage, he cut off two of the three ports he had promised them, so that the length and discomfort of the passage might reduce some to compliance — or that he might, by squeezing them all into one place, more conveniently carry out what he had designed: which was to seize every child under fourteen from the arms of their fathers and mothers, transporting them out of sight and contact, into a place where they could be instructed and brought up in our religion. He says this produced a most horrid spectacle. The natural affection between parents and children, and beyond that their zeal for their ancient belief, fighting against this violent decree, fathers and mothers were commonly seen killing themselves; and, by a still more terrible example, throwing their own young children into wells and pits out of love and compassion, to escape the severity of the law. As for the rest, when the appointed time expired, for lack of means to transport them they fell back into slavery. Some also turned Christian, but on whose faith — and on that of their descendants, even today, a hundred years on — few Portuguese yet feel they can rely; though custom and length of time are far more powerful counsellors in such changes than any other constraint. In the town of Castelnaudari, fifty heretic Albigensians let themselves be burned alive in a single fire rather than renounce their views.

Who sold the Jews banished from Castile a retreat in his dominions for eight crowns a head and a fixed term, and after the term made slaves of those who stayed.

What, moreover, about pain — which Aristippus, Hieronymus, and most of the sages have reputed the worst of all evils; and which even those who have denied it in words have admitted in their conduct? Posidonius, racked with a sharp and painful disease, was visited by Pompey, who apologised for having come at such a bad moment to hear him discourse on philosophy. ## modern-en · foulke-of-anjou · 40:52

William, our last Duke of Guienne, the father of that Eleanor who carried the duchy into the houses of France and England, wore continuously for the last ten or twelve years of his life a suit of armour under a religious habit, by way of penance. Foulke, Count of Anjou, went all the way to Jerusalem to have himself whipped there by two of his servants, with a rope around his neck, before the sepulchre of our Lord. But don't we still, every Good Friday in various places, see great numbers of men and women beating and whipping themselves until they tear and cut the flesh to the very bone? I have often seen it, and without any trick to it; and it was said that there were some among them (they go disguised) who for money undertook by this means to bear the religious penance of others, by a contempt of pain all the greater because the incentives of devotion are more powerful than those of greed. Q. Maximus buried his son when he was consul, M. Cato his when praetor-elect, and L. Paulus both of his within a few days of each other, all of them with a countenance that showed no kind of grief. I once said jokingly of a certain man that he had cheated divine justice; for the violent death of three of his grown children was sent to him on a single day, as a severe scourge, presumably; and so far from being afflicted by it, he took it for a particular grace and favour of heaven. I do not go in for these monstrous humours, although I lost two or three children at nurse, if not without grief at least without complaint, and there is hardly an accident that cuts closer to the quick. I see many other grounds of sorrow that, if they happened to me, I would barely feel; and I have despised some, when they have come on me, to which the world has given so terrible a figure that I would blush to boast of my equanimity.

Who went to Jerusalem to have himself whipped by two of his servants, with a cord about his neck, before the sepulchre.

One man being led to the gallows told his guards they must not take him through such-and-such a street, in case a merchant who lived there should stop him on the way over an old debt. Another told the hangman not to touch his neck because he was ticklish and would burst out laughing. Another, told by his confessor that he would sup with our Lord that very day, said, "You go in my place; I myself am fasting today." Another, having called for a drink, when the hangman drank first, said he would not drink after him for fear of catching some disease. Everyone has heard the tale of the Picard, who, standing on the ladder, was offered a common wench — the law sometimes allowing this — being told that if he would marry her his life would be spared. He looked her over for a while, noticed that she limped, and said, "Come on, string me up, string me up; she limps." They tell a similar story of a man in Denmark, condemned to lose his head, who was offered the same bargain on the scaffold and refused, because the girl on offer had hollow cheeks and too sharp a nose. A servant in Toulouse, accused of heresy, when asked what he believed referred himself to the belief of his master, a young student who was a fellow prisoner, choosing rather to die than allow himself to be persuaded that his master could be wrong. We read that when Louis XI took the city of Arras, a great many of its inhabitants let themselves be hanged rather than say "God save the King." And even among that mean-souled tribe, the buffoons, there have been some who would not stop fooling around at the very moment of death. One, as the hangman was launching him off the ladder, cried out "Launch the galley!" — one of his stock sayings. Another, lying at the point of death on a bed of straw set before the fire by his friends, was asked by the doctor where the pain lay. "Between the bench and the fire," he said. When the priest, coming to give him extreme unction, was groping for his feet — which the pain had made him pull up under him — he said, "You'll find them at the end of my legs." To someone present urging him to commend himself to God, he said, "Why, who's going there?" — and the man replied, "You will be presently, if such is His pleasure." "Am I sure to be there by tomorrow night?" he asked. "Just commend yourself to Him," the other said, "and you'll be there soon enough." "Then I'd best," said he, "carry my own recommendations."

Foulke, Count of Anjou, went all the way to Jerusalem to have himself whipped there by two of his servants, with a rope around his neck, before the sepulchre of our Lord. But don't we still, every Good Friday in various places, see great numbers of men and women beating and whipping themselves until they tear and cut the flesh to the very bone? I have often seen it, and without any trick to it; and it was said that there were some among them (they go disguised) who for money undertook by this means to bear the religious penance of others, by a contempt of pain all the greater because the incentives of devotion are more powerful than those of greed. Q. Maximus buried his son when he was consul, M. Cato his when praetor-elect, and L. Paulus both of his within a few days of each other, all of them with a countenance that showed no kind of grief. I once said jokingly of a certain man that he had cheated divine justice; for the violent death of three of his grown children was sent to him on a single day, as a severe scourge, presumably; and so far from being afflicted by it, he took it for a particular grace and favour of heaven. I do not go in for these monstrous humours, although I lost two or three children at nurse, if not without grief at least without complaint, and there is hardly an accident that cuts closer to the quick. I see many other grounds of sorrow that, if they happened to me, I would barely feel; and I have despised some, when they have come on me, to which the world has given so terrible a figure that I would blush to boast of my equanimity.

Who buried his son when the son was praetor elect with a countenance that expressed no manner of grief; and who, as consul, forbade the inhabitants of some Spanish cities to wear arms, whereupon a great many of them killed themselves. Not the Cato of Utica to whom Montaigne gives a chapter.

## modern-en · feraulez · 40:83

Feraulez, a man who had gone through both fortunes, and found that the increase of property was no increase of appetite — whether for eating, drinking, sleeping, or the enjoyment of his wife — and who on the other hand felt the care of his economics weighing heavily on his shoulders, as it does on mine, decided to do a favour to a poor young man, his loyal friend, who hankered after wealth; and made him a gift of all that he had, which was excessively great, and moreover of all he was going to receive day by day from the generosity of Cyrus, his good master, and from the war, on condition that he would handsomely maintain him and entertain him liberally as his guest and friend. This being done accordingly, they afterwards lived very happily together, both of them equally content with the change of their condition. It is an example I could imitate with all my heart; and I very much approve of the fortune of the aged prelate whom I see to have so completely stripped himself of his purse, his revenue, and the care of his expenses, committing them now to one trusty servant, now to another, that he has spun out a long succession of years, by this means as ignorant of his domestic affairs as any stranger.

Who had run through both fortunes and found that increase of substance was no increase of appetite, and gave away the great estate he had got by Cyrus’s liberality and the war, on condition only that he be handsomely maintained.

## modern-en · dionysius-the-younger · 40:75

My second condition of life was to have money of my own; I managed things so that I soon laid up a considerable sum out of a modest fortune, on the principle that what one really owns is what one sets aside out of one's ordinary spending, and that one cannot absolutely rely on revenue one only hopes to receive, however clear the hope may be. "For what," I said, "if I should be caught short by some accident?" And after such empty and vicious imaginings, I would very wisely, by this hoarding, provide against all eventualities; and could, moreover, answer those who objected that the number of these was too vast that, if I couldn't lay up for all, I could at least do it for some, and for many. Yet this was not done without a great deal of solicitude and anxiety. I kept it very close, and though I dare to talk so boldly about myself, I never spoke truly of my money — but falsely, as others do, who being rich pretend to be poor, and being poor pretend to be rich, dispensing their consciences from ever telling sincerely what they have: a ridiculous and shameful prudence. Was I going on a journey? It seemed to me I was never well enough provided; and the more I loaded myself with money, the more I loaded myself with fear — one moment about the danger of the roads, the next about the loyalty of the man in charge of my baggage; of whom, like some others I know, I was never sufficiently sure unless I kept him constantly in view. If I happened to leave my cash-box behind, oh, what strange suspicions and anxieties I fell into, and, what was worse, without daring to share them with anybody. My mind was eternally taken up with such things; so that, all in all, there is more trouble in keeping money than in earning it. And even if I didn't really do all I say, or wasn't really as ridiculously anxious about my money as I've made out, it still cost me something at least to restrain myself from being so. I drew little or no advantage from what I had, and my expenses seemed no less to me for having more to spend; for, as Bion said, hairy men are as angry as bald men at being plucked. Once you are used to it and have set your heart on your hoard, it is no longer at your service: you can't bring yourself to break into it. It's like a building you fancy must inevitably collapse to ruin if you so much as stir a single pebble; necessity must take you by the throat before you will bring yourself to touch it. I would sooner have pawned anything I owned, or sold a horse, and with much less reluctance, than have made the slightest breach in that beloved purse I had so carefully laid by. But the danger is that a man cannot easily set certain limits to this desire (they are hard to find for things one takes to be good), and to hold this good husbandry short of degenerating into miserliness. People are forever intent on adding to the heap, and increasing the stock from sum to sum, until at last they vilely deprive themselves of the enjoyment of their own goods, and put everything in reserve without making any use of it at all. By this rule the richest people in the world are those set to guard the walls and gates of a wealthy city. All money-men, I conclude, are misers. Plato sets out the corporal or human goods in this order: health, beauty, strength, riches; and riches, he says, are not blind, but very clear-sighted, when illuminated by prudence. Dionysius the Younger did a very fine thing on this subject; he was informed that one of his Syracusans had hidden a treasure in the ground, and sent word for him to bring it. The man brought it, secretly keeping back only a small part for himself, with which he went off to another city, where, having been cured of his appetite for hoarding, he began to live in a more liberal style. When Dionysius heard of it, he had the rest of the treasure returned to him, saying that since the man had learned to use it, he was very willing to give it back.

Dionysius the son, who heard that a Syracusan had hidden a treasure, sent for it, and afterwards gave it back when he found the man had learned to live without it.
