## modern-en · catulus-luctatius · 41:7

And yet we have some examples of just that. Catulus Luctatius in the Cimbrian war, having done all he could to make his fleeing soldiers turn and face the enemy, finally fled with them himself, faking the coward, so that his men would look as though they were following their captain rather than running from the enemy — sacrificing his own reputation in order to cover the shame of others. When Charles V came into Provence in 1537, it is said that Antonio de Leva, seeing the emperor firmly resolved on the expedition and believing it would do him great honour, nevertheless very stiffly opposed it in council, so that the entire glory of the resolution would be attributed to his master, and it could be said his own wisdom and foresight were such that, against everyone else's opinion, he had brought about so great an enterprise — which was to do him honour at his own expense. The Thracian ambassadors, coming to console Archileonida, the mother of Brasidas, on the death of her son, and praising him to the point of saying he had left no equal behind him, she rejected this private and particular praise to attribute it to the public: "Don't tell me that," she said. "I know the city of Sparta has many citizens both greater and of greater worth than he." In the battle of Crécy, the Prince of Wales, then very young, had been given command of the vanguard; the brunt of the battle happened to fall in that part of the field, which led the lords with him, finding themselves overmatched, to send to King Edward to come up to their relief. He asked how his son was, and being told he was alive and on horseback: "Then I'd do him wrong," said the king, "to go and rob him of the honour of winning this battle he has sustained so long and so bravely. Whatever risk he runs, the honour shall be entirely his own." And accordingly he would neither come up himself nor send help, knowing that if he went, it would be said all would have been lost without his rescue, and the honour of the victory would be wholly given to him.

Who in the Cimbrian war, having done all that lay in him to make his flying soldiers face about, ran away with the rest and counterfeited the coward, so that his men might seem to follow their captain rather than to fly from the enemy — abandoning his own reputation to cover the shame of others.

## modern-en · theopompus · 41:10

Many at Rome thought, and often said, that the greatest of Scipio's deeds were in part due to Laelius, whose constant practice it was always to advance and uphold Scipio's grandeur and renown without any care for his own. And Theopompus, king of Sparta, said to a man who told him the republic couldn't fail because he himself knew so well how to command: "It's rather," he replied, "because the people know so well how to obey." Just as women who succeeded to peerages had, despite their sex, the privilege of attending and voting in trials within the jurisdiction of the peers, so the ecclesiastical peers, despite their profession, were obliged to attend our kings in their wars, not just with their friends and servants but in person. The Bishop of Beauvais did so when he was with Philip Augustus at the battle of Bouvines, where he played a notable part in the action; but he didn't think it fitting for him to share in the fruit and glory of that violent and bloody trade. He took several of the enemy that day with his own hand and turned them over to the first gentleman he met, leaving it to him either to kill them or to accept their surrender, referring the whole execution to that other hand. He did this with the Earl of Salisbury, William, whom he handed over to Messire Jehan de Nesle. By a similar subtlety of conscience to the one I have just mentioned, he would kill but not wound, and so always fought with a mace. And a certain person of my own time, being reproached by the king for having laid hands on a priest, flatly and positively denied any such thing — meaning he had cudgelled and kicked him.

King of Sparta, who answered the man who told him the republic could not miscarry since he knew so well how to command: it is rather because the people know so well how to obey.

## modern-en · mercury · 42:18

In Thrace the king was set apart from his people in a rather pleasant and peculiar manner: he had a religion to himself, a god all his own — whom his subjects were not allowed to worship — which was Mercury, while he himself disdained to have anything to do with theirs, Mars, Bacchus, and Diana. And yet these are merely pictures that make no essential difference. For just as you see actors in a play playing the part of a duke or an emperor on stage, and immediately afterward go back to their true original condition of valets and porters, so the emperor, whose pomp and lustre so dazzle you in public:

The god the king of Thrace kept to himself, having a religion by himself and a god all his own which his subjects were not to presume to adore.

King Alfonso used to say that in this respect asses were better off than kings, since their masters let them feed at their own ease and pleasure — a favour that kings cannot get from their servants. And it has never occurred to me that it could be of any great benefit to the life of a man of sense to have twenty people gabbling around him while he is on the privy; or that the services of a man worth ten thousand livres a year, or who has taken Casale or defended Siena, should be either more comfortable or more acceptable to him than those of a good groom of the chamber who knows his job. The advantages of sovereignty are in a manner only imaginary; every degree of fortune has in it some image of principality. Caesar calls all the lords of France, who hold their lands in free franchise, roitelets or petty kings; and in truth, the title of "sire" excepted, they go pretty far toward kingship. Just look in the provinces remote from court — Brittany, for example — and notice the train, the vassals, the officers, the employments, the service, the ceremony, and the state of a lord who lives retired from court in his own house, among his own tenants and servants; and observe besides the flight of his imagination: there is nothing more royal; he hears talk of his master once a year, as of a king of Persia, with no further acknowledgment of him than through some remote kinship his secretary keeps track of in some register. And, to tell the truth, our laws are easy enough — so easy that a French gentleman scarcely feels the weight of sovereignty pressing on his shoulders more than twice in his life. Real and effective subjection only touches those among us who voluntarily put their necks under the yoke, and who aim at wealth and honours through such services: for a man who loves his own fireside, and can manage his household without falling out with his neighbours or getting tangled up in lawsuits, is as free as the Doge of Venice.

## modern-en · otho · 44:0

Reason directs that we should always go the same way, but not always at the same pace. And though a wise man ought not to give such free rein to human passions as to let them deviate from the right path, he may, without prejudice to his duty, leave it to them to hurry or to slow his speed, and not fix himself like a motionless and unfeeling Colossus. If virtue itself could put on flesh and blood, I believe the pulse would beat faster going on to an assault than going on to dinner: that is, there is a necessity that she should warm up and be stirred on this occasion. I have noticed, as something extraordinary, certain great men who in the highest enterprises and most important affairs have kept themselves in such a settled and serene calm as not to disturb their sleep. Alexander the Great, on the day fixed for that furious battle between him and Darius, slept so deeply and so long in the morning that Parmenio was forced to come into his chamber and, standing by his bedside, call him by name several times — the hour to go and fight compelling him to do so. The Emperor Otho, having resolved to kill himself that night, after settling his domestic affairs, dividing his money among his servants, and putting a good edge on a sword he had chosen for the purpose, and now waiting only to be sure that all his friends had got safely away, fell into so sound a sleep that the gentlemen of his chamber heard him snore. The death of this emperor has in it circumstances paralleling that of the great Cato, and particularly this just-mentioned one: for Cato, ready to dispatch himself, holding his hand only in expectation of the return of a messenger he had sent to bring word whether the senators he had sent away had got clear of the port of Utica, fell into so sound a sleep that those in the next room heard him snore; and when the man he had sent to the port had woken him to tell him that stormy weather had prevented the senators from putting to sea, he sent off another messenger, and composing himself again in bed, settled to sleep, and slept until the return of the last messenger brought him certain news that they were gone. We may further compare him with Alexander in the great and dangerous storm that threatened him through the sedition of the tribune Metellus, who, attempting to publish a decree to call Pompey with his army into the city at the time of Catiline's conspiracy, was opposed only — and stoutly — by Cato, so that very sharp language and bitter threats passed between them in the senate on the matter. But it was the next day, in the forenoon, that the controversy was to be decided, where Metellus, besides the favour of the people and of Caesar — at that time of Pompey's faction — was to appear accompanied by a rabble of slaves and gladiators; and Cato fortified only with his own courage and constancy; so that his relatives, household, and many of his virtuous friends were in great fear for him, to the point that some passed the whole night without sleep, eating, or drinking, for the danger they saw him in; his wife and sisters did nothing but weep and torment themselves in his house. He, on the contrary, comforted everyone, and after supping in his usual way, went to bed and slept soundly till morning, when one of his fellow tribunes roused him to go to the encounter. The knowledge we have of the greatness of this man's courage from the rest of his life may surely warrant us in judging that his composure came from a soul so far raised above such accidents that he disdained to let them take any more hold on his imagination than any ordinary incident.

Who, resolved to kill himself that night, settled his domestic affairs, divided his money among his servants, set a good edge on the sword he had chosen, waited only to be satisfied that his friends had got away safe, and then fell into so sound a sleep that the gentlemen of his chamber heard him snore. Vitellius’s insults to his soldiers afterwards did what their own captains could not, and made them fall upon the man who had offered them.

## modern-en · sextus-pompeius · 44:1

In the naval engagement that Augustus won against Sextus Pompeius in Sicily, just as the battle was about to begin, he was so fast asleep that his friends had to wake him to give the signal for the fight: this was what gave Mark Antony occasion afterwards to reproach him that he hadn't the courage so much as to look on the order of his own squadrons with open eyes, and hadn't dared to show himself to the soldiers until Agrippa had brought him news of the victory won. But as for young Marius, who did much worse (on the day of his last battle against Sulla, after he had drawn up his army and given the word and signal for battle, he lay down under the shade of a tree to rest himself, and fell so soundly asleep that the rout and flight of his men could barely wake him, having seen nothing of the fight), he is said to have been at that time so utterly worn out with labour and lack of sleep that nature could hold out no longer. Now, on what has been said, the physicians may decide whether sleep is so necessary that our lives depend on it; for we read that King Perseus of Macedon, being a prisoner at Rome, was killed by being kept from sleep; but Pliny gives examples of people who have lived long without it. Herodotus speaks of nations where the men sleep and wake by half-years; and those who write the life of the sage Epimenides assert that he slept fifty-seven years on end.

Whom Augustus beat in the naval engagement in Sicily that Augustus slept through, until his friends woke him to give the signal of battle.

## modern-en · machanidas · 45:1

Our battle of Dreux is striking for several extraordinary incidents — though those who have little affection for M. de Guise, and care little for his reputation, are eager to blame him. They say his halt, his delay with the forces under his command while the Constable, who was general of the army, was being raked through and through by the enemy's artillery, his battalion routed, himself taken prisoner — is inexcusable. He would have done much better, they argue, to risk a flank charge than to wait for the chance to fall on the enemy's rear, and so suffer such a heavy and consequential loss. But quite apart from what the outcome later showed, anyone who weighs the case without passion or prejudice will readily admit that the aim of a captain — and indeed of every private soldier — should be the overall victory, and that no particular incident, however close to his own interest, should pull him from that pursuit. Philopoemen, in an encounter with Machanidas, had sent out a strong party of his archers and slingers to open the skirmish. They were routed and hotly pursued by the enemy, who, riding their luck and chasing the rout, swept past the battalion where Philopoemen was stationed. His own men were straining to attack, but he refused to leave his post or to expose himself to relieve them. He let his archers be cut down before his eyes, and then, when he saw the enemy foot left unprotected by their cavalry, charged in. Even though they were Lacedaemonians, he caught them at the very moment when, thinking the victory secured, they were beginning to break their ranks. He destroyed them with ease and then set off in pursuit of Machanidas. The case is very like Monsieur de Guise's.

Whom Philopoemen fought, and who let his own horse run off in pursuit past the battalion where Philopoemen stood: Philopoemen suffered his archers and slingers to be chased and cut in pieces before his face rather than leave his post, then charged the enemy’s foot when the horse had left it unprotected, and afterwards put himself in pursuit of Machanidas.

Another item: there is a saying that it is good to have a good name, meaning credit and a good reputation. ## modern-en · nicholas-denisot · 46:12

the chase here is very much in earnest: which of these letters is to be rewarded for so many sieges, battles, wounds, imprisonments, and services rendered to the crown of France by this famous constable? Nicholas Denisot never bothered himself with anything beyond the letters of his name, whose order he scrambled to build up by anagram the Count d'Alsinois, on whom he handsomely settled the glory of his own poetry and painting. The historian Suetonius was satisfied with just the sense of his name, and dropped his father's surname Lenis to leave Tranquillus as heir to his reputation. Who would believe that Captain Bayard has no honour but what he derives from the deeds of Peter Terrail; or that Antonio Iscalin should sit and watch himself robbed, to his face, of the honour of so many sea voyages and commands by sea and land under the names of Captain Paulin and the Baron de la Garde? Second, these strokes of the pen are common to thousands of people. How many in each family share the same name and surname? And how many more in different families, ages, and countries? History tells us of three Socrateses, five Platos, eight Aristotles, seven Xenophons, twenty Demetrii, twenty Theodores — and we can guess how many more she never met. What is to stop my stable-boy from calling himself Pompey the Great? But when all is done, what virtue, what authority, what secret machinery is there that pins onto my dead stable-boy, or onto the other Pompey whose head was cut off in Egypt, this glorious renown and these so honoured flourishes of the pen, to their advantage?

Who altered the whole contexture of the letters of his own name to build up the Count d’Alsinois by anagram, and then handsomely endowed that figure with the glory of his poetry and his painting.

## modern-en · sertorius · 47:14

In the same way, if one had to decide whether soldiers should be lavishly and sumptuously dressed or armed only as the immediate task requires, the argument for the first might run as follows — and Sertorius, Philopoemen, Brutus, Caesar, and others held this view: that fine attire inflames a soldier's courage and is a spur to him; and that it also makes him fight more stubbornly, since his arms are in effect his estate and his whole inheritance to defend. This is why, says Xenophon, the men of Asia carried their wives and concubines, with their best jewels and richest possessions, with them to the wars. But the arguments would line up just as readily on the other side: that a general ought to reduce, not enlarge, his men's anxiety about saving themselves; that fine equipment makes them doubly afraid to risk their persons, and serves as a double temptation to the enemy to fight more resolutely where such booty and rich spoils are to be had. The thing was famously observed in earlier times as a powerful incentive to the Romans against the Samnites. Antiochus, showing Hannibal the army he had raised — marvellously splendid and rich in every kind of equipage — asked him whether the Romans would be satisfied with that army. "Satisfied?" replied Hannibal. "Yes, no doubt — however great their greed." Lycurgus not only forbade his soldiers all manner of finery in their gear but also forbade them to strip the enemies they defeated, because he wanted, as he said, poverty and frugality to shine alongside the rest of the battle.

One of the captains of the opinion that a soldier richly and sumptuously accoutred is the more inflamed with courage and the more obstinate in fight, having his arms, which are in a manner his whole inheritance, to defend.

## modern-en · vitellius · 47:15

At sieges and on other occasions where we come up close to the enemy, we readily let our men taunt, abuse, and revile him with every kind of injurious language. There is some colour of reason in this: it is no small thing to strip them of all hope of mercy or terms by reminding them that no quarter is to be expected from an enemy they have provoked so far, and that no remedy is left except victory. And yet Vitellius found himself fooled by this approach. He had to deal with Otho's soldiers, who were weaker in valour, long unused to war and softened by the pleasures of Rome. He stung them at last with so much abuse — reproaching them with cowardice and with regret for the mistresses and entertainments they had left behind in the city — that he inspired them with a resolution no exhortation could have produced, and made them fall upon him with a fury their own captains had been unable to rouse in them. And indeed, when the injuries cut to the quick, it can easily happen that the man who was going reluctantly to fight on his prince's behalf will pitch in with another kind of spirit when the quarrel becomes his own.

Who so nettled Otho’s soldiers with injurious language, reproaching them with cowardice and with the mistresses and entertainments they had left behind at Rome, that he inspired them with a resolution no exhortation had had the power to give them, and made them fall upon himself.

## modern-en · levinus · 47:16

Considering how important it is to keep the general of an army alive, and that the enemy's whole aim is directed straight at the head on which all the rest depend, the course taken by so many great captains — changing their dress and disguising themselves just before engaging — seems past dispute. And yet the inconvenience a man runs into by doing so is no less than the one he thinks to avoid. The captain, hidden from the recognition of his own men, no longer has the courage his presence and example would have inspired in them; not seeing the familiar marks and ensigns of their leader, they soon conclude that either he is dead or, despairing of the business, has gone off to look after himself. And experience shows both methods have succeeded and failed. What happened to Pyrrhus in the battle he fought against the Consul Levinus in Italy will serve to illustrate both points. By hiding himself in Megacles's armour and giving Megacles his own, he undoubtedly saved his life — but by that very means he came very close to the other disaster of losing the battle. Alexander, Caesar, and Lucullus loved to be recognisable in a fight by rich equipment and armour of a particular gleam and colour. Agis, Agesilaus, and that great Gilippus, on the contrary, used to fight without any display, with no imperial escort or distinguishing marks.

The consul against whom Pyrrhus fought in Italy on the day the king shrouded his person in Megacles’s armour.

## modern-en · clearchus · 47:17

Among the other faults laid to Pompey's charge at Pharsalia, he is reproached for keeping his army standing still to receive the enemy's charge — "because by doing so" (I will here lift Plutarch's own words, which are better than mine) "he deprived himself of the violent impact that running adds to the first shock of arms, and he prevented that crash of the combatants into one another that usually gives them greater impetuosity and fury, especially when they rush in with full force, their courage rising with the shouts and the run. He chilled the soldiers' ardour, as it were, and made it more reserved." That is what Plutarch says. But if Caesar had come off worse, why might not someone else have argued the reverse — that the strongest and steadiest fighting stance is one in which a man is planted firm, without motion; that those who hold steady on the march, closing up and reserving their strength for the moment of action, have a great advantage over men who are disordered, who have already spent half their breath running headlong into the charge. Besides, an army is a body made up of so many individual members that it is impossible for it to move at that pace without breaking the order of battle, and without the leading men being engaged before their comrades can come up to help them. In that unnatural battle between the two Persian brothers, the Lacedaemonian Clearchus, who commanded the Greeks on Cyrus's side, led them on softly and without haste toward the charge, but when they were within fifty paces he hurled them on at full speed, hoping in so short a run to keep order and save their wind and at the same time to give weight and impetus both to their persons and to their missile weapons. Others have settled the question for their own armies this way: if your enemy comes at you full tilt, stand firm to receive him; if he stands still to receive you, charge him full tilt.

The Lacedaemonian who commanded the Greeks of Cyrus’s party in the unnatural battle between the two Persian brothers, and led them on softly and without precipitation until they came within fifty paces, and then hurried them full speed — hoping in so short a career to keep their order, husband their breath, and still give the advantage of impetuosity to their persons and their missile arms.

## modern-en · artybius · 48:3

There are many horses trained to help their riders so well that they will rush at anyone who shows a drawn sword, and fall on whoever faces or opposes them with mouth and hoofs. But they often do more harm to their friends than to their enemies; and once they are engaged and locked on you cannot get them off and back into order, so that you are left at the mercy of their fight. It went very badly for Artybius, general of the Persian army, in a single combat with Onesilus, king of Salamis, to be mounted on a horse trained like this; it was the cause of his death, since Onesilus's squire chopped the horse down with a scythe between the shoulders as it was rearing up over his master. And what the Italians report — that at the battle of Fornova the horse of Charles VIII, kicking and plunging, freed his master from the enemies pressing on him, without which he would have been killed — sounds like an enormous piece of luck, if it is true.

General of the Persian army, whose horse was trained to rear and fall with mouth and heels on whoever fronted it. Fighting man to man with Onesilus, that training was the occasion of his death, for it gave Onesilus’s squire the chance to cleave the horse down between the shoulders with a scythe as it reared over his master.

I would gladly forgive our people for taking no pattern or rule of perfection but their own particular manners and customs — for it is a common vice, not just of the common run but of nearly all men, to walk in the beaten road their ancestors trod before them. I am content that, when they see a Fabricius or a Laelius, they think his face and bearing barbarous, since he is neither dressed nor groomed in our manner. But what I find fault with is their singular thoughtlessness in letting themselves be so blinded and bullied by the authority of present fashion that they change their opinions every month, if custom requires it, and revise their judgments on questions that touch them personally. When they wore the busk of their doublets up to their breasts, they stiffly insisted that was its proper place; a few years later, when it had slipped down between the thighs, they could laugh at the old fashion as uncomfortable and unbearable. The fashion now in use leads them to condemn both of the other two with such firm conviction and such universal consent that you would think a kind of madness had crept in among them, blinding their understanding to this strange degree. Now, given that our turnover of fashions is so prompt and abrupt that all the tailors in the world cannot dream up enough new whim-whams to feed our vanity, it must often happen that the discarded styles come back in again, and then drop into the same contempt; and that the same judgment, in fifteen or twenty years, will pass through half a dozen not only different but contradictory opinions, with an unbelievable lightness and inconstancy. Not one of us is so discerning as not to be taken in by this contradiction and, both in external and internal sight, blinded without realising it.

## modern-en · sancho-xii · 54:3

I have just come from playing with my own family at a game of finding the most things that touch at both extremities. "Sire," for instance, is a title given to the greatest man in the nation, the king, and also to the lowliest, like merchants — but never to anyone of any rank in between. Women of high birth are called Dames, lesser gentlewomen Demoiselles, and the meanest sort of women Dames again, like the first. The cloth of state above our tables is allowed only in the palaces of princes and in taverns. Democritus said that gods and beasts have sharper senses than men, who are in the middle. The Romans wore the same clothes at funerals and at feasts. It is quite certain that extreme fear and an extreme rush of courage both equally trouble and loosen the bowels. The nickname "the Trembling" by which they called Sancho XII, king of Navarre, tells us that valour will set the limbs trembling just as fear does. Those who were arming that king — or whoever else, on a like occasion, was apt to fall into the same agitation — tried to settle him down by playing down the danger he was about to face. "You don't understand me," he said, "for if my flesh could know the danger my courage will straight away carry it into, it would sink to the ground." The faintness that overtakes us in the exercises of Venus, from coldness or distaste, also comes from too violent a desire and an immoderate heat. Extreme cold and extreme heat both scald and roast. Aristotle says that lead pigs will melt and run with cold and the harshness of winter just as with a strong heat. Desire and satiety fill all the gradations above and below pleasure with pain. Stupidity and wisdom meet at the same midpoint of feeling and resolution in the bearing of life's accidents: the wise master and triumph over ill, the others never know it; the latter, you might say, sit on this side of the accidents, the former go beyond them, having weighed and considered their character, measured and judged them for what they are, and then, by force of a vigorous soul, leapt out of their reach; they look down on them and trample them underfoot, having a solid and well-fortified soul against which the darts of fortune, when they come to strike, must necessarily rebound and blunt themselves, meeting a body in which they can make no impression. The ordinary middling sort of men are lodged between these two extremes, made up of those who notice their evils, feel them, and are not able to bear them. Infancy and decrepitude meet in the weakness of the brain; avarice and prodigality meet in the same thirst and desire to get.

King of Navarre, surnamed Trembling. Being armed for a fight and shaking, and being told by way of comfort that the danger was less than he thought: you understand me ill, he said — could my flesh know the danger my courage will presently carry it into, it would sink to the ground.

## modern-en · king-david · 56:11

It is not without very good reason, in my opinion, that the Church forbids the casual, indiscreet, and irreverent use of the holy and divine Psalms with which the Holy Ghost inspired King David. We are not to mix God into our actions except with the highest reverence and caution; that poetry is too holy to be put to no other use than exercising the lungs and pleasing the ears; it ought to come from the conscience, not from the tongue. It is not right that an apprentice in his shop, among his vain and frivolous thoughts, should be allowed to pass the time and amuse himself with such sacred things. Nor is it decent to see the Holy Book of the holy mysteries of our belief tossed about a hall or a kitchen — they used to be mysteries, but have now become sport and recreation. It is a book too serious and too venerable to be turned over carelessly or lightly; the reading of Scripture ought to be a measured and deliberate act, to which men should always add this devout preface, sursum corda, preparing even the body with so humble and composed a bearing and look as will show particular reverence and attention. Nor is it a book for everyone to handle, but for the study of select men set apart for the purpose, and whom Almighty God has been pleased to call to that office and sacred function: the wicked and the ignorant grow worse from it. It is not a tale to tell but a history to revere, fear, and adore. Are they not amusing men, then, who think they have made it fit for the people's handling by translating it into the vernacular? Does the whole understanding of what is in it hang on the words? Dare I go further and say that by drawing this near to understanding a little of it, they fall much wider of the whole scope than before? A pure and simple ignorance, wholly depending on the exposition of qualified persons, was far more learned and more salutary than this vain and verbal knowledge, which has only rashness and presumption to it.

## modern-en · theodosius · 56:13

One of our Greek historians justly criticises the age he lived in, because the secrets of the Christian religion were scattered into the hands of every mechanic to expound and argue over as he saw fit, and says we ought to be much ashamed — we who by God's special favour enjoy the pure mysteries of piety — to let them be profaned by the ignorant rabble; considering that the pagans expressly forbade Socrates, Plato, and the other sages to inquire into or even so much as mention the things entrusted to the priests of Delphi. He says further that the factions of princes on theological subjects are armed not with zeal but with fury; that zeal springs from divine wisdom and justice and governs itself with prudence and moderation, but degenerates into hatred and envy, producing tares and nettles instead of grain and wine, when it is driven by human passions. And it was well said by another, who, advising the Emperor Theodosius, told him that disputes did not so much rock the schisms of the Church to sleep as rouse and animate heresies; that therefore all contentions and dialectical disputes were to be avoided, and men were to acquiesce wholly in the formulas of faith laid down by the ancients. And the Emperor Andronicus, having overheard some great men at high words with Lapodius in his palace about a point of ours of great importance, gave them so sharp a check as to threaten to have them thrown into the river if they did not stop. The very women and children nowadays presume to lecture the oldest and most experienced men on the ecclesiastical laws; whereas the first of those of Plato forbids them even to inquire into the civil laws, which were to stand in place of divine ordinances; and, allowing the old men to confer among themselves or with the magistrate about such things, he adds — provided it not be in the presence of the young or of profane persons.

The emperor whom an adviser told that disputation did not rock the schisms of the Church asleep but roused and animated heresies, and that men should acquiesce in the formulas of faith the ancients had established.

He says further that the factions of princes on theological subjects are armed not with zeal but with fury; that zeal springs from divine wisdom and justice and governs itself with prudence and moderation, but degenerates into hatred and envy, producing tares and nettles instead of grain and wine, when it is driven by human passions. And it was well said by another, who, advising the Emperor Theodosius, told him that disputes did not so much rock the schisms of the Church to sleep as rouse and animate heresies; that therefore all contentions and dialectical disputes were to be avoided, and men were to acquiesce wholly in the formulas of faith laid down by the ancients. And the Emperor Andronicus, having overheard some great men at high words with Lapodius in his palace about a point of ours of great importance, gave them so sharp a check as to threaten to have them thrown into the river if they did not stop. The very women and children nowadays presume to lecture the oldest and most experienced men on the ecclesiastical laws; whereas the first of those of Plato forbids them even to inquire into the civil laws, which were to stand in place of divine ordinances; and, allowing the old men to confer among themselves or with the magistrate about such things, he adds — provided it not be in the presence of the young or of profane persons.

The emperor who, overhearing some great men at high words in his palace with Lapodius about a point of theology, checked them so severely as to threaten to have them thrown into the river if they did not desist.

## modern-en · st-chrysostom · 56:16

I have also known, in my time, some men whose writings were faulted for being purely human and philosophical, with no admixture of theology; and yet with some show of reason the opposite case might be made — that divine doctrine, as queen and regent of the rest, better keeps her state apart; that she ought to be sovereign throughout, not subsidiary and ancillary; that perhaps grammatical, rhetorical, and logical examples may be more fittingly chosen from elsewhere, as may the material for the stage, the games, and public entertainments, than from so sacred a matter; that divine reasons are considered with greater reverence and attention by themselves and in their own proper style, than when mingled with and adapted to human discourse; that it is a fault more often noticed that the divines write too humanly than that the humanists write not theologically enough. Philosophy, says St. Chrysostom, has long been banished from the holy schools as a handmaid altogether useless and unworthy even to look in passing by the door into the sanctuary of the holy treasures of the celestial doctrine; that the human way of speaking is of a much lower form and ought not to take on for itself the dignity and majesty of divine eloquence. Let anyone who pleases talk in verbis indisciplinatis of fortune, destiny, accident, good and ill luck, and other such phrases, according to his own bent; for my part I propose fancies merely human and merely my own, and I propose them simply as human fancies, considered separately, not as settled by any decree from heaven, beyond doubt or dispute — matter of opinion, not matter of faith; things which I discuss according to my own notions, not as I believe according to God; in a lay, not a clerical fashion, and yet always in a very religious manner, as children prepare their exercises — not to instruct, but to be instructed.

Who says that philosophy has long been banished the holy schools as a handmaid altogether useless, and thought unworthy to look so much as in passing by the door into the sanctuary of the celestial doctrine.

## modern-en · boniface-viii · 58:0

Those who make it their business to scrutinise human actions find nothing so confounding as the effort to reconcile them and present them to the world with one consistent lustre and reputation; for they commonly contradict one another so strangely that it seems impossible they could proceed from one and the same person. We find the younger Marius one moment a son of Mars, the next a son of Venus. Pope Boniface VIII, it is said, entered his papacy like a fox, conducted himself in it like a lion, and died like a dog. And who could believe it was the same Nero, the very image of cruelty, who, having the sentence of a condemned man brought to him to sign, as was the custom, cried out, "Oh that I had never been taught to write!" — so much did it grieve him to condemn a man to death? History is full of such examples, and every man can produce so many from his own practice or observation that I sometimes wonder to see thoughtful men go to the trouble of sorting these pieces, when irresolution appears to me the most common and obvious vice of our nature — witness the famous line of the playwright Publius:

Who entered into his Papacy like a fox, it is said, behaved himself in it like a lion, and died like a dog.

## modern-en · lucretia · 58:15

We fluctuate between various inclinations; we will nothing freely, nothing absolutely, nothing constantly. In any man who had set down clear laws and rules in his head for his own conduct, we would notice a steadiness of manner, an order, a sure relation of one thing and action to another, shining through his whole life. Empedocles observed this very disparity in the people of Agrigentum: they gave themselves up to pleasure as if every day were their last and built as if they were going to live forever. The judgment is not hard to make, as is very evident in the younger Cato; whoever has found one step in him will be led to all the rest — it is a harmony of perfectly tuned notes that cannot jar. With us it is quite the opposite: every particular action requires a particular judgment. The surest course to steer by, in my opinion, would be to take our measure from the nearest related circumstances, without engaging in a longer inquiry or drawing any larger conclusion. I was told, during the civil disorders of our poor kingdom, that a girl, near where I was then staying, had thrown herself out of a window to avoid being forced by a common soldier billeted in the house. She was not killed by the fall, and so, repeating her attempt, she would have cut her own throat had she not been stopped. Still, having wounded herself enough to look in real danger, she freely confessed that the soldier had so far only pestered her with courtship, urgent solicitation, and gifts, but that she was afraid he would in the end resort to violence — all of which she delivered with such a look and accent, soaked moreover in her own blood (the highest testimony of her virtue), that she seemed another Lucretia. Yet I have since been well assured that, both before and after, she was not such a difficult piece. And, as the innkeeper says in Ariosto, however handsome a man and worthy a gentleman you may be, do not conclude too much about your mistress's inviolable chastity just because you were turned away — for all you know, she may have a better stomach for your muleteer.

The Roman whom the maid of Montaigne’s neighbourhood appeared another of, having thrown herself from a window and then at her own throat to escape a soldier — until Montaigne was very well assured that both before and after she was not so difficult a piece.

## modern-en · clytus · 58:28

No valour can be more extreme of its kind than Alexander's; but it is of just one kind, not full enough throughout, not universal. Incomparable as it is, it has its blemishes. His being so often at his wits' end on the slightest suspicion of his captains plotting against his life, and conducting that inquiry with so much vehemence and rash injustice, with a fear that wrecked his natural reason — that is one telling instance. And the superstition with which he was so tainted carries with it a certain image of cowardice; the excess of his remorse over the killing of Clytus is another testimony to the unevenness of his courage. All we perform is no more than a patchwork, so to speak, of various pieces, and we would acquire honour under a false title. Virtue cannot be followed except for itself; if it sometimes borrows her mask for some other purpose, she promptly tears it off again. It is a vivid and powerful tint that, once the soul has truly absorbed it, will not come out except with the cloth. And so, to judge a man rightly, we must follow his trace long and with close observation. If constancy does not stand firm there on her own proper base —

Whose murder Alexander’s excess of penitence for is one of Montaigne’s testimonies to the unevenness of that great courage.

## modern-en · attalus · 59:21

I would not have believed there could be so deep, senseless, and dead a degree of drunkenness if I had not read in history that Attalus, in order to put a notable insult upon him, invited to supper the same Pausanias who afterwards killed Philip of Macedon — a king whose excellent qualities testified well enough to his education in the household and company of Epaminondas — and made him drink to such a pitch that he could afterwards hand over his beauty, as if he were a roadside whore, to the muleteers and the basest servants of the house. And I have been further told, by a lady whom I highly honour and esteem, that near Bordeaux and around Castres, where she lives, a countrywoman, a widow of chaste reputation, finding in herself the first signs of pregnancy, told her neighbours innocently that if she had a husband she would think herself with child. But as the grounds for suspicion grew daily, until at last it became plain fact, the poor woman was driven to have it proclaimed in her parish church that whoever had done the deed and would freely confess could not only be forgiven but, if he liked, married. Whereupon a young fellow who served her as a labourer, encouraged by the proclamation, declared that one holiday he had found her — having taken too much of the bottle — so fast asleep by the fireplace and in so indecent a posture that he could conveniently do his business without waking her. And they live to this day as man and wife.

Who, to put a notable affront upon Pausanias, invited him to supper and made him drink to such a pitch that he could afterwards abandon his beauty, as of a hedge strumpet, to the muleteers and servants of the basest office in the house.

## modern-en · anaxarchus · 59:51

— when Anaxarchus, on the order of Nicocreon, tyrant of Cyprus, was placed in a stone mortar and pounded with iron mauls, never stopped saying, "Strike, batter, break — it is not Anaxarchus, it is only his sheath you pound and crush"; when we hear our martyrs cry out to the tyrant from the middle of the flame, "This side is roasted enough — fall to and eat, it is well done; now set to work on the other"; when we hear the child in Josephus, torn piecemeal with pincers, defy Antiochus and cry out in a steady, assured voice, "Tyrant, you waste your effort — I am still at ease. Where is the pain? Where are the torments with which you so threatened me? Is this all you can do? My constancy torments you more than your cruelty does me. Pitiful coward, you weaken and I grow stronger; make me complain, make me bend, make me yield if you can; encourage your guards, cheer up your executioners — see, see, they faint and can do no more; arm them, goad them, spur them on" — one must confess that there is some frenzy, some fury, however holy, possessing those souls at such a moment. When we come to these Stoical sallies — "I had rather be mad than voluptuous," says Antisthenes; when Sextius tells us he had rather be fettered by affliction than by pleasure; when Epicurus presumes to play with his gout, and, refusing health and ease, defies all torments, despising the lesser pains as beneath his contest, hungering and calling out for others sharper, more violent, and more worthy of him —

Who, put into a stone mortar by command of Nicocreon and laid upon with mauls of iron, did not cease to say: strike, batter, break — it is not Anaxarchus, it is but his sheath that you pound and bray so.

Pitiful coward, you weaken and I grow stronger; make me complain, make me bend, make me yield if you can; encourage your guards, cheer up your executioners — see, see, they faint and can do no more; arm them, goad them, spur them on" — one must confess that there is some frenzy, some fury, however holy, possessing those souls at such a moment. When we come to these Stoical sallies — "I had rather be mad than voluptuous," says Antisthenes; when Sextius tells us he had rather be fettered by affliction than by pleasure; when Epicurus presumes to play with his gout, and, refusing health and ease, defies all torments, despising the lesser pains as beneath his contest, hungering and calling out for others sharper, more violent, and more worthy of him —

Who says he had rather be fettered with affliction than with pleasure.

## modern-en · damidas · 60:3

When Philip had forcibly entered the Peloponnese and someone said to Damidas that the Lacedaemonians stood likely to suffer greatly if they did not in time reconcile themselves to his favour, "Why, you wretched fellow," he replied, "what can they suffer who do not fear to die?" Agis, too, was asked how a man might live free. "Why," he said, "by despising death." These, and a thousand other sayings to the same effect, plainly mean more than patiently awaiting the stroke of death when it comes — for there are several accidents of life worse to suffer than death itself. Witness the Lacedaemonian boy captured by Antigonus and sold as a slave who, when his master ordered him to some base task, said, "You shall see whom you have bought — it would be a shame for me to serve, when liberty is within my reach," and so saying, threw himself from the top of the house. When Antipater severely threatened the Lacedaemonians, the better to bring them to grant a demand of his, they replied, "If you threaten us with worse than death, we shall die more willingly"; and to Philip, who had written that he would frustrate all their undertakings, "What, will you also stop us from dying?" This is the meaning of the saying that the wise man lives as long as he ought, not as long as he can; and that the most obliging present nature has given us, and which removes all colour for complaining of our condition, is that she has placed the keys of life in our own keeping. She has provided only one door into life, but a hundred thousand ways out. We may be cramped for earth to live on, but earth enough to die on can never be wanting, as Boiocalus answered the Romans. Why complain of this world? It does not detain you; your own cowardice is the cause if you live in pain. There needs no more to die than to will to die:

To whom someone said that the Lacedaemonians were likely to suffer much if they did not reconcile themselves to Philip in time: why, you pitiful fellow, he replied, what can they suffer who do not fear to die?

## modern-en · therykion · 60:35

Among those of the first of these two opinions, there has been great debate as to what occasions are sufficient to justify deliberate self-murder, which they call "a reasonable exit." For though they say that men must sometimes die for trivial causes, since those that detain us in life are of no great weight either, yet there must be some limit. There are fantastic and senseless impulses that have driven not only individual men but whole nations to destroy themselves, of which I have given examples elsewhere. We also read of the Milesian virgins, who by a mad compact hanged themselves one after another until the magistrate took order in it, decreeing that the bodies of any found so hanged should be drawn naked through the city by the same halter. When Therykion tried to persuade Cleomenes to dispatch himself because of the ill posture of his affairs and, having missed a more honourable death in the lost battle, to accept this second-best one rather than give the conquerors leisure to inflict on him either a shameful death or a degrading life, Cleomenes, with a courage truly Stoic and Lacedaemonian, rejected his advice as unmanly and base: "That," he said, "is a remedy that will never be unavailable, but one a man should not resort to while an inch of hope remains." He told him that it was sometimes constancy and valour to live; that he wanted even his death to be of use to his country, and would make of it an act of honour and virtue. Therykion, nevertheless, thought himself in the right and did his own business; and Cleomenes did the same afterwards, but only after he had first tried out the utmost malice of fortune. Not all the troubles in the world are weighty enough to make a man die to dodge them; and besides, there are so many sudden and unexpected changes in human affairs that it is hard to judge rightly when we are at the end of our hope:

Who tried to persuade Cleomenes to despatch himself after the battle he had lost, rather than give the conquerors leisure to make him undergo an ignominious death or an infamous life — and, his counsel being rejected as unmanly and mean, went and did his own business.

## modern-en · democritus-aetolian · 60:45

Seneca says only those which keep on disturbing the functions of the soul for a long time. And there have been some who, to avoid a worse death, have chosen one of their own liking. Democritus, general of the Aetolians, brought as a prisoner to Rome, found a way to escape by night; but, hotly pursued by his keepers, he fell on his own sword and died rather than let himself be retaken. Antinous and Theodotus, when their city of Epirus was reduced by the Romans to the last extremity, advised the people to kill themselves universally. The people preferring to give themselves up to the enemy, the two chiefs went to seek the death they wanted, rushing furiously upon the enemy with intent to strike home but not to ward off any blow. When the Island of Gozzo was taken some years ago by the Turks, a Sicilian who had two beautiful marriageable daughters killed them both with his own hand, along with their mother who ran in to save them; that done, he sallied out of the house with a crossbow and arquebus, killed with two shots the two Turks nearest his door, and drawing his sword charged furiously among the rest, where he was quickly surrounded and cut to pieces — by that means delivering his family and himself from slavery and dishonour. The Jewish women, after circumcising their children, threw them and themselves down a precipice to escape the cruelty of Antigonus. I have been told of a man of rank in one of our prisons whose friends, hearing that he would certainly be condemned, suborned a priest to tell him — to spare him the disgrace of such a death — that the only means of his deliverance was to commend himself to such-and-such a saint under such-and-such vows, and to fast eight days together without taking any nourishment, whatever weakness or faintness he might feel. He followed their advice, and so destroyed himself before he was aware, not suspecting death or any danger in the experiment. Scribonia, advising her nephew Libo to kill himself rather than wait for the stroke of justice, told him that to keep his life only to put it after into the hands of those who within three or four days would haul him to execution was to do other people's business, and that to keep his blood for them to gratify their malice was to serve his enemies.

General of the AEtolians, brought prisoner to Rome, who escaped by night and, closely pursued by his keepers, fell upon his own sword rather than be retaken. Not the philosopher of Abdera.

## modern-en · nicanor · 60:46

We read in the Bible that Nicanor, the persecutor of the law of God, having sent his soldiers to seize the good old man Razis — surnamed, for his virtue, the father of the Jews — the good man, seeing no other remedy, his gates burned down and the enemies ready to take him, chose to die nobly rather than fall into the hands of his wicked adversaries and let himself be cruelly butchered by them, contrary to the honour of his rank. He stabbed himself with his own sword, but in haste the blow had not gone home; so he ran and threw himself headlong from the top of a wall on the men below. They moved apart and made room, and he landed straight on his head. Yet, feeling still in himself some remains of life, he renewed his courage, sprang up on his feet all bloody and wounded, and making his way through the crowd to a steep rock, drew out his bowels through one of his wounds and, tearing and pulling them apart with both hands, threw them among his pursuers, all the while calling on divine vengeance for their cruelty and injustice.

The persecutor of the law of God who sent his soldiers to seize Razis.

History is everywhere full of people who, by a thousand routes, have exchanged a painful and tedious life for death. Lucius Aruntius killed himself, he said, to flee both the future and the past. Granius Silvanus and Statius Proximus, after being pardoned by Nero, killed themselves — either disdaining to live by the favour of so wicked a man, or so as not to be troubled at some other time to seek a second pardon, given the readiness of his nature to suspect and credit accusations against worthy men. Spargapises, son of Queen Tomyris, taken prisoner of war by Cyrus, used the first favour Cyrus showed him — ordering him untied — to kill himself, claiming no other benefit of liberty than to be revenged upon himself for the disgrace of having been captured. Boges, governor of Eion for King Xerxes, besieged by the Athenian army under Cimon, refused the terms offered (a safe return into Asia with all his wealth), unable to bear surviving the loss of a post his master had given him to keep. So, after defending the city to the last extremity, when nothing was left to eat, he first threw all the gold and everything else the enemy could plunder into the river Strymon, then ordered a great pyre lit and the throats cut of all the women, children, concubines, and servants, whose bodies he threw into the fire, and at last leaped into it himself.

Who killed himself to fly, he said, both the future and the past.

Spargapises, son of Queen Tomyris, taken prisoner of war by Cyrus, used the first favour Cyrus showed him — ordering him untied — to kill himself, claiming no other benefit of liberty than to be revenged upon himself for the disgrace of having been captured. Boges, governor of Eion for King Xerxes, besieged by the Athenian army under Cimon, refused the terms offered (a safe return into Asia with all his wealth), unable to bear surviving the loss of a post his master had given him to keep. So, after defending the city to the last extremity, when nothing was left to eat, he first threw all the gold and everything else the enemy could plunder into the river Strymon, then ordered a great pyre lit and the throats cut of all the women, children, concubines, and servants, whose bodies he threw into the fire, and at last leaped into it himself.

The other of the two pardoned men who did that.

## modern-en · ninachetuen · 60:51

Ninachetuen, an Indian lord, at the first whisper that the Portuguese Viceroy meant to strip him, with no clear cause, of his command in Malacca, in order to transfer it to the King of Campar, took this resolution: he had a scaffold built, longer than broad, supported by columns royally hung with tapestry and strewn with flowers and abundant perfumes; and when all was ready, he came out into the street in a robe of cloth of gold studded with jewels of great value, and mounted the steps to the scaffold, at one corner of which he had a pyre of aromatic wood lit. Everyone ran to see what these unusual preparations were for; whereupon Ninachetuen, with a manly but indignant air, set out how much he had served the Portuguese nation, and with how unspotted fidelity he had behaved in his charge; that, having so often, sword in hand, shown for others that honour was much dearer to him than life, he was not to abandon care for it on his own behalf; that, since fortune denied him any way of resisting the affront prepared for him, his courage at least required him to free himself from the feeling of it, and not to become a tale told by the people or a triumph to men less deserving than himself. Having said this, he leaped into the fire.

An Indian lord who, hearing the first whisper that the Portuguese Viceroy meant to take his command in Malacca from him without apparent cause and give it to the King of Campar, built a scaffold hung with tapestry and strewn with flowers, came out in cloth of gold set with jewels, set out from it how much he had obliged the Portuguese nation and with how unspotted a fidelity, said that fortune denying him all means of opposing the affront his courage at least enjoined him to free himself from the sense of it, and leapt into the fire he had lighted at one corner.

## modern-en · sextilia · 60:52

Sextilia, wife of Scaurus, and Paxaea, wife of Labeo, to encourage their husbands to escape the dangers pressing upon them — in which they had no share but conjugal affection — voluntarily sacrificed their own lives to serve them in this extreme necessity for company and example. What they did for their husbands, Cocceius Nerva did for his country, with less utility though with equal devotion: this great lawyer, flourishing in health, wealth, reputation, and favour with the emperor, had no other reason to kill himself but the bare pity of the miserable state of the Roman Republic. Nothing can be added to the beauty of the death of the wife of Fulvius, a familiar favourite of Augustus. Augustus, having discovered that he had divulged an important secret entrusted to him, received him very coldly one morning when he came to court and looked grimly at him. Fulvius returned home in despair and told his wife sorrowfully that, having fallen into this misfortune, he was resolved to kill himself; to which she answered roundly, "It is only right that you should, since after so often experiencing the looseness of my tongue you would not take warning. But let me kill myself first" — and without saying more she ran herself through the body with a sword. Vibius Virrius, despairing of the safety of his city, besieged by the Romans, and of their mercy, in the last debate of his city's senate, after many arguments to the same end, concluded that the noblest way to escape fortune was by their own hands. He told them the enemy would have them in honour, and Hannibal would feel how many faithful friends he had abandoned, and invited those who approved his advice to come to a good supper he had ready at home, where, after they had eaten well, they would all drink together of what he had prepared — "a drink," he said, "that will deliver our bodies from torments, our souls from insult, and our eyes and ears from feeling the many hateful evils the conquered suffer from cruel and implacable conquerors." He said he had arranged for proper persons to throw their bodies on a funeral pyre before his door as soon as they were dead. Many approved this high resolution, but few imitated it. Twenty-seven senators followed him, who, after having tried to drown the thought of this fatal decision in wine, ended the feast with the deadly mess; and embracing one another, after lamenting together their country's misfortune, some withdrew home to their own houses, others stayed to be burned with Vibius on his funeral pyre. All were so long in dying — the vapour of the wine having clogged the veins and so deferred the effect of the poison — that some of them came within an hour of seeing the enemy inside the walls of Capua, which was taken the next morning, and of undergoing the miseries they had at so dear a rate tried to avoid. Jubellius Taurea, another citizen of the same place, when the Consul Fulvius was returning from the shameful butchery of two hundred and twenty-five senators, called him back fiercely by name and, having stopped him, said, "Give the word that someone may dispatch me too, after the slaughter of so many others, so that you may boast of having killed a much braver man than yourself." Fulvius, dismissing him as a madman, and also having received letters from Rome censuring the inhumanity of his execution that tied his hands, Jubellius went on: "Since my country has been taken, my friends are dead, and I have with my own hands killed my wife and children to spare them the desolation of this ruin, and I am denied to die the death of my fellow citizens, let me borrow from virtue vengeance on this hated life" — and drawing a short sword he had hidden on him, he ran it through his own breast, falling backward and dying at the consul's feet.

Wife of Scaurus, who with Paxaea voluntarily sacrificed her own life to encourage her husband to avoid the dangers pressing upon him, in which she had no other share than conjugal affection.

Jubellius Taurea, another citizen of the same place, when the Consul Fulvius was returning from the shameful butchery of two hundred and twenty-five senators, called him back fiercely by name and, having stopped him, said, "Give the word that someone may dispatch me too, after the slaughter of so many others, so that you may boast of having killed a much braver man than yourself." Fulvius, dismissing him as a madman, and also having received letters from Rome censuring the inhumanity of his execution that tied his hands, Jubellius went on: "Since my country has been taken, my friends are dead, and I have with my own hands killed my wife and children to spare them the desolation of this ruin, and I am denied to die the death of my fellow citizens, let me borrow from virtue vengeance on this hated life" — and drawing a short sword he had hidden on him, he ran it through his own breast, falling backward and dying at the consul's feet.

Who told the senate of his besieged city that the noblest means of escaping fortune was by their own hands, and invited those who approved to a good supper with a beverage prepared after it. ## modern-en · cleombrotus · 60:57

But men sometimes covet death out of hope of a greater good. "I desire," says St. Paul, "to be with Christ," and "who shall rid me of these bands?" Cleombrotus of Ambracia, after reading Plato's Phaedo, conceived so great a desire for the life to come that, without any other occasion, he threw himself into the sea. In a certain kingdom of the newly discovered world, on a day of solemn procession when the idol they worship is drawn in public on a chariot of marvellous size, besides the many seen cutting off pieces of their flesh to offer to it, there are others who throw themselves down in its path, to be crushed and broken to pieces under the heavy wheels, to obtain after death the veneration of sanctity — which is duly paid them. The death of the bishop, sword in hand, has more magnanimity in it and less sensation, since the heat of battle takes away part of the latter.

The Sieur de la Brousse, my brother, and I, travelling one day together during the time of our civil wars, met a gentleman of good standing. He was of the opposite party, though I did not know it, for he pretended otherwise. The trouble in this kind of war is that the cards are so shuffled — your enemy not distinguished from yourself by any obvious mark of language or dress, having been raised under the same laws, climate, and manners — that it is very hard to avoid confusion and disorder. This made me afraid of meeting any of our own troops in a place where I was not known, that I might not be in fear to tell my name, and perhaps worse — as had happened to me before, when by such a mistake I lost both men and horses, including an Italian gentleman, my page, whom I had bred with the greatest care and affection, in whom a youth of great promise was wretchedly extinguished. But the gentleman my brother and I met had so desperate, half-dead a fear of meeting any horsemen or passing by any of the towns that held for the King, that I at last realised it was the alarm of conscience. The poor man felt as if through his visor and the crosses on his cassock one might have seen into his bosom and read the most secret intentions of his heart — so wonderful is the power of conscience. It makes us betray, accuse, and fight against ourselves, and for want of other witnesses, give evidence against ourselves:

Montaigne’s brother, travelling with him one day during the civil wars when they met the gentleman whose half-dead fear at every passing horse Montaigne at last discovered to be alarms of conscience.

There are a thousand examples of this; but three of one and the same person will be enough. Scipio, being accused one day before the people of Rome of crimes of a very high nature, instead of excusing himself or flattering his judges, said, "It will be a fine thing for you to sit in judgment on a head by whose means you have the power to judge all the world." Another time, to a string of impeachments brought against him by a tribune of the people, instead of making his defence he said, "Let us go, citizens — let us go and give thanks to the gods for the victory they gave me over the Carthaginians on this day," and walking off ahead toward the temple, he had presently the whole assembly, and his accuser himself, following at his heels. And when Petilius, put up to it by Cato, demanded an account of the money that had passed through his hands in the province of Antioch, Scipio, coming into the senate for that purpose, produced from under his robe a book in which, he told them, was an exact account of his receipts and disbursements; but when he was asked to hand it over to the prothonotary for examination, he refused, saying he would not do himself so great a disgrace, and in the presence of the whole senate tore the book in pieces with his own hands. I do not believe that the most calloused conscience could have counterfeited so great an assurance. He had naturally too high a spirit and was used to too high a fortune, says Titus Livius, to know how to be guilty, and to lower himself to the meanness of defending his innocence. The putting of men to the rack is a dangerous invention, and seems to be more a trial of patience than of truth. Both the man who has the fortitude to endure it conceals the truth, and the man who has not — for why should pain sooner make me confess what is, than force me to say what is not? And on the other hand, if the man who is not guilty of what he is accused of has the courage to undergo those torments, why should not the guilty man have the same, when so fair a reward as life is in his sights? I believe the basis of this invention comes from considering the force of conscience: for in the guilty man it seems to assist the rack in making him confess his fault and shake his resolution; and in the innocent it fortifies him against the torture. But, all said, it is in plain truth a trial full of uncertainty and danger. What would not a man say, what would not a man do, to avoid such unbearable torments?

Whom Cato set on to demand an account of the money that had passed through Scipio’s hands in the province of Antioch.

Julius Canus, a noble Roman of rare constancy and virtue, had been condemned to death by that worthless creature Caligula. What are you thinking of?" — "I was thinking," he answered, "of how to hold myself ready, with my faculties settled and fixed, to see whether in this short, quick instant of death I could catch the motion of the soul as she leaves the body, and whether she feels anything in the parting; so that, if I could, I might come back afterwards and report it to my friends." This man philosophises not just up to death but in death itself. A noble Roman condemned to die by Caligula who, going to the stroke, was asked by a philosopher friend what his soul was doing, and answered that he was keeping his mind settled and fixed to try whether in that short and quick instant he could perceive the motion of the soul as she parted from the body — and come back, if he could, to tell his friends of it.

## modern-en · hortensius · 63:41

This is, instead of blowing the child's nose, cutting it off altogether. I think the cure is worse than the disease. But granting that it must be sheer presumption to entertain people with talk about oneself, still, pursuing my general design, I cannot refrain from an action that publishes this weakness of mine, nor conceal a fault which I not only practise but profess. To speak my mind freely, however, I think that the habit of condemning wine because some people get drunk on it is itself to be condemned; we can only abuse what is good in itself, and I believe that this rule only has the popular vice in view. These are bridles for calves, with which neither the saints — whom we hear speaking so freely about themselves — nor the philosophers, nor the theologians let themselves be curbed; and neither will I, who am as little of the one as the other. If they do not write of themselves expressly, at least when the occasion calls for it they do not hesitate to step out into the open. What does Socrates discourse on more than himself? To what does he more often direct and steer the conversation of his disciples, than to speak of themselves — not of the lesson in their book, but of the substance and motion of their souls? We confess ourselves religiously to God and our confessor; and to our neighbours, in front of everyone. But some will answer that there we say nothing but accusations against ourselves. Why then, we are saying everything; for our very virtue itself is faulty and porous. My trade and my art is to live; anyone who forbids me to speak according to my own sense, experience, and practice might as well order an architect to speak of building not from his own knowledge but from his neighbour's, by someone else's knowledge and not his own. If it is vainglory for a man to publish his own virtues, why does Cicero not prefer the eloquence of Hortensius, and Hortensius that of Cicero? Perhaps they mean that I should give testimony of myself by works and effects, not just by words. What I mostly paint is my thoughts, a subject without shape and incapable of producing visible results; it is all I can do to give it body in this airy form of the voice. The wisest and most devout men have lived in great care to avoid any showy effects. Effects would speak more of fortune than of me; they show their own face, not mine, and only uncertainly, by inference; they are samples of one particular virtue. I expose myself entire. It is a body in which, at a single view, the veins, muscles, and tendons all appear, each in its place — here the effects of a cold, there of a beating heart, very tentatively. I do not write my deeds; I write myself and my essence.

The orator whose eloquence Montaigne asks why Cicero does not prefer to his own, if it is vainglory for a man to publish his own virtues — and why Hortensius does not prefer Cicero’s.

## modern-en · monsieur-destissac-husband · 65:2

Now, madam, having to draw my own portrait to the life, I would have left out an important feature if I had not also represented the honour I have always had for you and your merits — which I have deliberately chosen to put at the start of this chapter, because, among the many other fine qualities you possess, the tender love you have shown your children stands very high. Whoever knows at what age Monsieur d'Estissac, your husband, left you a widow; the great and honourable matches that have since been offered to you, as many as to any lady of your rank in France; the constancy and steadiness with which, for so many years, you have borne so many sharp difficulties, the burden and conduct of business that has hounded you in every corner of the kingdom, and is not yet tired of harassing you; and the happy result you have given to all of it, by your own prudence or good fortune — anyone who knows all that will easily agree with me that we have no more vivid example of maternal devotion in our times than yours. I thank God, madam, that it has been so well placed; for the great hopes that Monsieur d'Estissac your son gives of himself are firm enough that when he comes of age you will harvest from him all the obedience and gratitude of a very good man. But since, on account of his tender years, he has not been able to take in those services of the highest value which he has received from you in such number, I want, if these papers should one day come into his hands when I no longer have mouth or speech to tell him myself, that he should receive from me a true account of what is being more effectively shown to him by its effects already: namely, that there is no gentleman in France more indebted to a mother's care, and that he cannot, in the future, give better or more certain proof of his own worth and virtue than by acknowledging you for the excellent mother that you are.

Her husband, who left her a widow young.

Whoever knows at what age Monsieur d'Estissac, your husband, left you a widow; the great and honourable matches that have since been offered to you, as many as to any lady of your rank in France; the constancy and steadiness with which, for so many years, you have borne so many sharp difficulties, the burden and conduct of business that has hounded you in every corner of the kingdom, and is not yet tired of harassing you; and the happy result you have given to all of it, by your own prudence or good fortune — anyone who knows all that will easily agree with me that we have no more vivid example of maternal devotion in our times than yours. I thank God, madam, that it has been so well placed; for the great hopes that Monsieur d'Estissac your son gives of himself are firm enough that when he comes of age you will harvest from him all the obedience and gratitude of a very good man. But since, on account of his tender years, he has not been able to take in those services of the highest value which he has received from you in such number, I want, if these papers should one day come into his hands when I no longer have mouth or speech to tell him myself, that he should receive from me a true account of what is being more effectively shown to him by its effects already: namely, that there is no gentleman in France more indebted to a mother's care, and that he cannot, in the future, give better or more certain proof of his own worth and virtue than by acknowledging you for the excellent mother that you are.

Her son, whose great hopes of himself render the account of her widowhood sufficient.

## modern-en · muley-hassam · 65:17

Muley Hassan, king of Tunis, the one whom the Emperor Charles V restored to his kingdom, reproached the memory of his father Mahomet with his frequenting of women, calling him loose, effeminate, and a begetter of children. The Greek histories tell us that Iccus the Tarentine, Chryso, Astyllus, Diopompos, and others, to keep their bodies in shape for the Olympic games and similar exercises, denied themselves during that training all dealings with Venus. In a certain country of the Spanish Indies men were not allowed to marry until after forty, yet the girls were given over at ten. It is not time for a gentleman of thirty to give place to his son of twenty; he is himself in a position to serve both in war and in the court of his prince; he needs all his resources; and yet, no doubt, he ought to surrender a share — but not so great a share as to forget himself for others. For such a man, the answer fathers usually have at the ready — "I will not take off my clothes before I go to bed" — serves well enough.

King of Tunis, whom the Emperor Charles restored, and Montaigne’s instance in that chapter. The modern edition spells him Hassan.
